b:temple_jupiter_om_v1.summary: The great Etruscan-plan temple of the Capitoline Triad, vowed by Tarquinius Priscus, built by Tarquinius Superbus and dedicated by the consul M. Horatius Pulvillus on 13 September 509 BC. The largest temple of its age in Italy: a cappellaccio podium about 53 x 62 m carrying a deep porch of three rows of six widely spaced tufa columns, three cellae (Jupiter in the wider central one, flanked by Juno and Minerva) and a timber superstructure clad in painted terracottas by Vulca of Veii, crowned by a terracotta quadriga (bronze from 296 BC).

phases.t: dedicated by M. Horatius Pulvillus on the Ides of September
survives the Gallic sack while the Capitol holds out
the Ogulnii replace the terracotta quadriga with bronze
columns and walls whitened with stucco by the censors
burns on 6 July with the Sibylline Books

Podium 53.5 x 62.25 m (Mura Sommella); Etruscan plan with triple cella and three rows of six columns in the pronaos, colonnades down the flanks, blind rear wall.

b:temple_jupiter_om_v2.summary: Rebuilt on the archaic foundations after the fire of 83 BC: Sulla began it, using marble column elements brought from the Olympieion at Athens, and Q. Lutatius Catulus dedicated it in 69 BC with gilded bronze roof tiles. Augustus restored it at great expense. It burned when the Vitellians stormed the Capitol in December 69.

Closed after 392; Stilicho stripped gold from the doors, Gaiseric carried off half the gilded tiles in 455, and it decayed into a quarry.

b:tabularium_v1.summary: The great substructure building closing the Forum at the foot of the Capitol, built by Q. Lutatius Catulus in 78 BC after the fire of 83: a sheer peperino and tufa wall with small windows supporting an arcaded gallery framed by Doric half-columns, with a lost upper storey. Long identified as the state record office; it more likely carried a monumental passage between Arx and Capitolium.

b:columna_rostrata_duilii.summary: Column hung with the bronze prows of the Carthaginian ships captured by C. Duilius at Mylae in 260 BC, Rome's first naval victory; the inscription was recut under Claudius.

fire on the Aventine side of the circus (Tac. Ann. 6.45)

b:circus_maximus_v8.summary: Tiberius paid for the damage of the fire of 36. Claudius replaced the tufa carceres with marble and the wooden metae with gilded bronze ones and reserved seats for senators. The Great Fire of July 64 broke out in the shops built against the circus on the Palatine side.

phases.t: Claudius: marble carceres, gilded metae, senatorial seats (Suet. Claud. 21.3)
Great Fire starts in the tabernae of the circus (Tac. Ann. 15.38)

scholarship: Humphrey, Roman Circuses: Arenas for Chariot Racing (1986) 56-294
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 84-87

Obelisk offsets are metres from the spina centre, positive toward the carceres (along rot).

b:circus_maximus_v9.summary: Rebuilt quickly after 64: Nero's triumph of 67-68 passed through it. In 81 the Senate set a triple arch to Titus across the entrance in the curved end. Damaged again by fire under Domitian, who began a full rebuilding.

phases.t: Arch of Titus built at the curved end (CIL VI 944)
Domitian begins rebuilding after a fire

scholarship: Humphrey, Roman Circuses: Arenas for Chariot Racing (1986) 56-294
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 84-87
Ciancio Rossetto, LTUR I (1993) 272-277 s.v. Circus Maximus

Obelisk offsets are metres from the spina centre, positive toward the carceres (along rot).

b:circus_maximus_v10.summary: Trajan completed the rebuilding in masonry around AD 103: an arcaded three-storey facade with shops, concrete vaults carrying the cavea, some 621 x 118 m overall with an arena about 580 x 79 m, seating at least 150,000 (Pliny claims 250,000, the Regionary Catalogues 385,000 places). The spina carried the obelisk, shrines, the egg and dolphin counters and the gilded metae. Under Antoninus Pius a collapse killed 1,112 people; another collapse under Diocletian killed some 13,000.

phases.t: rebuilding finished by Trajan (Pliny Pan. 51; CIL VI 955)
partial collapse of the stands under Antoninus Pius (SHA Ant. 9.1)
collapse during Diocletian's reign (Chron. 354)

scholarship: Humphrey, Roman Circuses: Arenas for Chariot Racing (1986) 56-294
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 84-87
Ciancio Rossetto, LTUR I (1993) 272-277 s.v. Circus Maximus
Coarelli, Rome and Environs (2007) 327-330
b:circus_maximus_v10.note: Overall size after Humphrey's reconstruction; outer facade height ~28 m for three arcaded storeys. Axis and centre from the outline of the Circo Massimo archaeological area (OSM relation 11384819): long axis bearing 126/306 deg; rot 306 = from the curved ESE end toward the WNW carceres. Obelisk offsets are metres from the spina centre, positive toward the carceres (along rot).

b:circus_maximus_v11.summary: In 357 Constantius II, on his only visit to Rome, raised on the spina the obelisk of Thutmose III from Karnak, 32.2 m, the tallest in the city, which Constantine had meant for Constantinople. The circus kept running through the fifth century and under Theodoric; the last races recorded were given by the Gothic king Totila in 549.

phases.t: second obelisk raised (Amm. Marc. 17.4.12-17)
last chariot races in Rome, under Totila (Procopius, Goth. 3.37.4)

scholarship: Humphrey, Roman Circuses: Arenas for Chariot Racing (1986) 56-294
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 84-87
Ciancio Rossetto, LTUR I (1993) 272-277 s.v. Circus Maximus
Coarelli, Rome and Environs (2007) 327-330

Axis and centre from the outline of the Circo Massimo archaeological area (OSM relation 11384819): long axis bearing 126/306 deg; rot 306 = from the curved ESE end toward the WNW carceres. Obelisk offsets are metres from the spina centre, positive toward the carceres (along rot).

b:circus_maximus_v12.summary: After 549 the circus fell out of use. The stands were quarried and the valley slowly silted up; the obelisks fell and were buried, to be dug up in 1587.

phases.t: no further games recorded

scholarship: Humphrey, Roman Circuses: Arenas for Chariot Racing (1986) 56-294

b:circus_maximus_v12.note: Stands left standing as a shell; height reduced for stripped upper tiers. Axis and centre from the outline of the Circo Massimo archaeological area (OSM relation 11384819): long axis bearing 126/306 deg; rot 306 = from the curved ESE end toward the WNW carceres. Obelisk offsets are metres from the spina centre, positive toward the carceres (along rot).

b:fornix_stertinii_circus.summary: Arch built by L. Stertinius in 196 BC from Spanish spoils, carrying gilded statues; one of three he set up, the others in the Forum Boarium.
scholarship: Richardson (1992) 154 s.v. Fornix Stertinii
Humphrey (1986) 97
b:fornix_stertinii_circus.note: Its place in the circus is unknown; put at the curved end where the later Arch of Titus stood, a common hypothesis. Ended at 80 on the assumption that the Titus arch replaced it.

b:arch_of_titus_circus_maximus_v1.summary: Triple arch voted by the Senate in 81 to Titus for the capture of Jerusalem, standing as the monumental entrance in the middle of the curved end of the circus. Its inscription was copied in the Einsiedeln itinerary; foundations and column fragments were excavated in 2014-2015.

phases.t: dedicated by Senate and People to Titus (CIL VI 944)

scholarship: Humphrey (1986) 97-100
Buonfiglio, Pergola and Zanzi, excavation reports on the Arch of Titus in the Circus Maximus (2015-2017)
b:arch_of_titus_circus_maximus_v1.note: Footprint about 17 x 15 m from the excavated foundations; height estimated with quadriga. rot points out of the circus (ESE); the arch is two-faced. Survived as a ruin into the Middle Ages.

b:pulvinar_circus_maximus_v1.summary: Augustus' shrine-like box on the Palatine side of the cavea where the images of the gods carried in the pompa circensis were set on cushions and where the emperor sat. Rebuilt with the cavea under Trajan.
scholarship: Humphrey (1986) 78-83
Richardson (1992) 322
b:pulvinar_circus_maximus_v1.note: Placed on the Palatine (+x) side about 30 m toward the carceres from the arena midpoint, opposite the finish line; faces SW into the arena.

b:temple_of_sol_circus_maximus_v1.summary: An old shrine of the Sun, patron of the circus, set into the seating on the Aventine side opposite the pulvinar; reliefs and mosaics of the circus show a small temple there, crowned by a statue of Sol. After Nero's escape from the Pisonian conspiracy in 65 offerings were made to Sol 'who has an old temple in the circus'.
scholarship: Humphrey (1986) 91-95
Richardson (1992) 363
b:temple_of_sol_circus_maximus_v1.note: Form from depictions (Foligno relief, Piazza Armerina mosaic); size estimated. Luna shared the cult in late sources.

b:ara_consi_v1.summary: The buried altar of Consus at the first turning post, uncovered only on the Consualia (21 August and 15 December) when races and mule-races were held; tied to the legend of the rape of the Sabine women.
scholarship: Humphrey (1986) 60-62
Richardson (1992) 100
b:ara_consi_v1.note: 'ad primas metas': placed at the eastern meta, following Humphrey's view that the first meta was the one at the curved end. Rendered as a low altar since it was normally covered.

b:sacellum_murciae_v1.summary: Ancient shrine of Murcia, later identified with Venus, that gave the valley (Vallis Murcia) and the eastern turning post (meta Murcia) their names; incorporated into the spina.
scholarship: Humphrey (1986) 95-97
Richardson (1992) 262
b:sacellum_murciae_v1.note: Placed near the eastern end of the spina.

b:temple_of_ceres_v1.summary: Vowed in 496 BC by the dictator A. Postumius during a famine and dedicated in 493 by Sp. Cassius to the plebeian triad Ceres, Liber and Libera. Vitruvius cites it as the type of the wide-spaced (araeostyle) Tuscan temple with terracotta pediment statues; the Greek artists Damophilos and Gorgasos decorated it. Seat of the plebeian aediles and their archive, and a refuge for the poor. Burned in 31 BC.

phases.t: dedicated by Sp. Cassius
burned in the fire of 31 BC (Dio 50.10.3)

scholarship: Richardson (1992) 80-81
Coarelli, Il Foro Boario (1988) 67-77
Spera, LTUR I (1993) 260-261
b:temple_of_ceres_v1.note: Dionysius (6.94.3) puts it 'directly above the carceres', i.e. at the western (Forum Boarium) end of the circus on the Aventine slope near S. Maria in Cosmedin, not at the curved end; placed accordingly. Facing NE toward the Palatine is assumed.

b:temple_of_ceres_v2.summary: Rebuilt by Augustus after the fire and dedicated by Tiberius in AD 17, keeping the old Tuscan form. Still standing in the Regionary Catalogues.
scholarship: Richardson (1992) 81

b:temple_of_flora_v1.summary: Built after consulting the Sibylline books by the plebeian aediles L. and M. Publicius Malleolus, near the circus, home of the licentious Floralia games.
scholarship: Richardson (1992) 152
b:temple_of_flora_v1.note: Tacitus: 'iuxta circum maximum'. Placed on the Aventine slope next to the Temple of Ceres; form and size conjectural.

b:temple_of_flora_v2.summary: Restored by Augustus and dedicated by Tiberius in AD 17 together with the Temple of Ceres.
scholarship: Richardson (1992) 152

b:temple_of_venus_obsequens_v1.summary: Built by Q. Fabius Gurges from fines levied on matrons convicted of adultery, the oldest temple of Venus in Rome, near the Circus Maximus.
scholarship: Richardson (1992) 409
b:temple_of_venus_obsequens_v1.note: 'ad Circum Maximum'; position along the Aventine flank of the circus and form conjectural.

b:temple_of_mercury_v1.summary: Dedicated in 495 BC by the centurion M. Laetorius, chosen by the people over the consuls, as seat of the merchants' guild (mercatores) overlooking the circus valley.
scholarship: Richardson (1992) 251
b:temple_of_mercury_v1.note: Ovid: 'templa spectantia Circum'. Position on the Aventine slope above the middle of the circus; presumably burned in 64.

b:temple_of_mercury_v2.summary: Rebuilt after the Neronian fire; a medallion of Marcus Aurelius showing a temple of Mercury with herm columns is often referred to a restoration.
scholarship: Richardson (1992) 251

b:temple_of_luna_aventine_v1.summary: Ancient temple of the Moon on the Aventine above the circus, ascribed to Servius Tullius; in 182 BC a gale blew its doors against the Temple of Ceres. Destroyed in the Great Fire of 64 and not heard of again.
scholarship: Richardson (1992) 238
b:temple_of_luna_aventine_v1.note: Livy's anecdote implies it stood above and close to the Temple of Ceres, near the top of the Clivus Publicius.

b:temple_of_iuventas_v1.summary: Vowed by M. Livius Salinator at the Metaurus (207) and dedicated in 191 BC 'ad Circum Maximum'. Burned in 16 BC.
scholarship: Richardson (1992) 228
b:temple_of_iuventas_v1.note: Placed on the Palatine flank near the carceres end; site unknown.

b:temple_of_iuventas_v2.summary: Restored by Augustus after the fire of 16 BC.
scholarship: Richardson (1992) 228

b:temple_of_summanus_v1.summary: Temple of the god of nocturnal thunder, dedicated during the war with Pyrrhus near the Circus Maximus; its terracotta statue on the pediment was struck by lightning in 278 BC.
scholarship: Richardson (1992) 376
b:temple_of_summanus_v1.note: 'ad Circum Maximum', side not known; placed on the Palatine flank.

b:temple_of_diana_aventine_v1.summary: The federal sanctuary of Diana of the Latins, ascribed to Servius Tullius in imitation of the Artemision of Ephesus; asylum, slaves' festival on the Ides of August, and archive of the Icilian law on the public land of the Aventine (456 BC) on a bronze pillar.

phases.t: lex Icilia de Aventino publicando set up here

scholarship: Richardson (1992) 108
Vendittelli, LTUR II (1995) 11-13
Platner-Ashby (1929) 149-150
b:temple_of_diana_aventine_v1.note: Location from Marble Plan fragment 22 as placed between S. Sabina and S. Prisca beside the Balneum Surae fragment (Digital Augustan Rome); Vendittelli's alternative site under S. Alessio rejected. Archaic form conjectural.

b:temple_of_diana_aventine_v2.summary: Rebuilt by L. Cornificius (consul 35 BC) after his triumph from Africa: an octastyle temple shown on the Severan Marble Plan inside a precinct with a double colonnade, labelled CORNIFICIA. Listed with Minerva in Regio XIII in the Regionary Catalogues; the Aventine was sacked in 410.
scholarship: Richardson (1992) 108
Rodriguez Almeida, Forma Urbis Marmorea (1981) pl. 15
Haselberger et al., Mapping Augustan Rome (2002) 108
b:temple_of_diana_aventine_v2.note: Plan from FUR fragment 22a-b (octastyle; dipteral form is one reading); size scaled from the fragment. Orientation conjectural.

b:temple_of_juno_regina_aventine_v1.summary: Vowed by M. Furius Camillus at the siege of Veii in 396 BC for Juno, Queen of Veii, whose cult statue was 'evoked' and carried to Rome; dedicated 1 September 392. Starting point of the matrons' procession of 207 BC with the hymn of Livius Andronicus.
scholarship: Richardson (1992) 216
Andreussi, LTUR III (1996) 125-126
b:temple_of_juno_regina_aventine_v1.note: Near the top of the Clivus Publicius by S. Sabina, where two inscriptions to Juno Regina (CIL VI 364-365) were found; exact site unknown.

b:temple_of_juno_regina_aventine_v2.summary: Restored by Augustus (Res Gestae 19); not mentioned afterwards.
scholarship: Richardson (1992) 216

b:temple_of_minerva_aventine_v1.summary: Seat of the guild of scribes and actors, honoured in 207 BC after Livius Andronicus' hymn; on the Aventine next to Diana.
scholarship: Richardson (1992) 255
b:temple_of_minerva_aventine_v1.note: Shown next to Diana on FUR fragment 22 (Digital Augustan Rome); placed NE of Diana. Founding date unknown, before 207 BC.

b:temple_of_minerva_aventine_v2.summary: Restored by Augustus; the Regionary Catalogues list a 'templum Dianae et Minervae' in Regio XIII.
scholarship: Richardson (1992) 255

b:temple_of_consus_aventine_v1.summary: Built by L. Papirius Cursor, triumphing over the Tarentines; his triumphal portrait in a toga picta was painted inside.
scholarship: Richardson (1992) 100

b:temple_of_vortumnus_v1.summary: Built by M. Fulvius Flaccus after the capture of Volsinii in 264 BC, the Etruscan god having been 'evoked' from the city; a painting of the triumphator in toga picta decorated it.
scholarship: Richardson (1992) 432
b:temple_of_vortumnus_v1.note: 'in vico Loreti Maioris', near the Diana precinct; exact site unknown.

b:temple_of_libertas_aventine_v1.summary: Built by Ti. Sempronius Gracchus from fines, with paintings celebrating his father's victory at Beneventum; restored by Augustus.
scholarship: Richardson (1992) 233

b:temple_of_bona_dea_subsaxana_v1.summary: Sanctuary of the women's goddess 'below the Rock' (Saxum) on the eastern slope of the Aventine, with medicinal herbs and tame snakes; men were barred.
scholarship: Richardson (1992) 59-60
b:temple_of_bona_dea_subsaxana_v1.note: Founding date unknown (tradition names a Vestal Claudia). Placed on the NE flank of the Aventine above the Piscina Publica area.

b:temple_of_bona_dea_subsaxana_v2.summary: Restored by Livia and later by Hadrian, whose works the Regionary Catalogues and the Historia Augusta record.
scholarship: Richardson (1992) 60

b:armilustrium_v1.summary: Open sacred area on the Aventine where the arms of the army were purified on 19 October at the end of the campaign season; said to hold the tomb of King Titus Tatius. Gave its name to the Vicus Armilustri.
scholarship: Richardson (1992) 44
b:armilustrium_v1.note: Placed near S. Sabina and S. Alessio along the street under Via di S. Sabina (Vicus Armilustri).

b:privata_traiani_v1.summary: Trajan's private house on the Aventine before his accession, listed in the Regionary Catalogues (Regio XIII). Rooms with early second-century paintings and mosaics found under Piazza del Tempio di Diana and the Casale Torlonia are the leading candidate; they were buried by the foundations of the Baths of Decius.
scholarship: Richardson (1992) 320
Coarelli, Rome and Environs (2007) 353
b:privata_traiani_v1.note: Identification with the remains under the Decian baths is one of two hypotheses (the other is the house under S. Prisca).

b:baths_of_decius_v1.summary: Small luxurious bath building for the aristocratic Aventine, built by the emperor Decius. Palladio drew its symmetrical plan, about 70 x 35 m with a central hall and an apsed room at the south corner; remains survive in the Casale Torlonia and under Piazza del Tempio di Diana.

phases.t: restored under Constantius and Constans

scholarship: Richardson (1992) 391
Coarelli, Rome and Environs (2007) 353
Palladio's drawing (Chatsworth), published by Lanciani
b:baths_of_decius_v1.note: Location between Piazza del Tempio di Diana and Via del Tempio di Diana from the Nolli map and inscriptions; the Wikipedia point (12.4843, 41.8833) lies too far east. Caldarium on the SW side for the afternoon sun; rot 225 = facing SW.

b:baths_of_decius_v2.summary: Restored after Alaric's sack by the urban prefect Caecina Decius Acinatius Albinus in 414, as an inscription records; later fate unknown.
scholarship: Richardson (1992) 391

b:baths_of_sura_v1.summary: Baths built by or for L. Licinius Sura, Trajan's marshal, next to his house on the Aventine and dedicated to Trajan; shown on the Severan Marble Plan (BALNEVM SVRAE) beside the Temple of Diana. Restored under Gordian III.

phases.t: restored under Gordian III

scholarship: Richardson (1992) 395
Rodriguez Almeida, Forma Urbis Marmorea (1981) frag. 21
b:baths_of_sura_v1.note: Placed NW of S. Prisca, along the street under Via di S. Prisca, per the traditional setting of FUR fragments 21-22; remains reported near the Accademia di Danza.

b:baths_of_sura_v2.summary: Repaired in 414 after the Gothic sack by Caecina Decius Acinatius Albinus.
scholarship: Richardson (1992) 395

b:domus_santa_prisca_v1.summary: A late first-century house with a nymphaeum and later a cult room, excavated under the church of S. Prisca in 1934-1966; variously identified with the house of Licinius Sura or with Trajan's private residence.
scholarship: Vermaseren and van Essen, The Excavations in the Mithraeum of the Church of Santa Prisca (1965)
Richardson (1992) 129
b:domus_santa_prisca_v1.note: Same footprint as the church above, which reused its walls.

b:mithraeum_santa_prisca_v1.summary: A Mithraic cave installed in the basement of the house under S. Prisca; a graffito gives the date of the founding as 20 November 202.
scholarship: Vermaseren and van Essen (1965)
b:mithraeum_santa_prisca_v1.note: Below ground; rendered as a small vault under the church site.

b:mithraeum_santa_prisca_v2.summary: Enlarged around 220 and repainted with the famous procession of the seven grades of initiates and their verses. Destroyed and filled in around 400, when the church was built above.
scholarship: Vermaseren and van Essen (1965)
Coarelli, Rome and Environs (2007) 352

b:dolichenum_aventine_v1.summary: Sanctuary of the Syrian Jupiter Dolichenus excavated in 1935 near Via di S. Domenico, with a rich deposit of sculpture and inscriptions of the second and third centuries.
scholarship: Richardson (1992) 221
Colini, Bullettino Comunale 63 (1935)
b:dolichenum_aventine_v1.note: Exact position approximate (Largo Arrigo VII / Via di S. Domenico area); plan generic.

b:domus_cilonis_v1.summary: Mansion given by Septimius Severus to his friend L. Fabius Cilo, city prefect, on the Little Aventine near the later Baths of Caracalla; listed in the Regionary Catalogues.
scholarship: Richardson (1992) 129
b:domus_cilonis_v1.note: Remains under or near S. Balbina have been suggested.

b:piscina_publica_v1.summary: A public swimming pool fed probably by the Aqua Appia, where the people went to swim and exercise; it gave its name to Regio XII but had disappeared by Festus' day.
scholarship: Richardson (1992) 297
b:piscina_publica_v1.note: Location in the valley between the Aventine and the Little Aventine north of the Baths of Caracalla; dates conjectural.

b:septizodium_v1.summary: A towering free-standing nymphaeum facade built by Septimius Severus in 203 at the SE corner of the Palatine, so that travellers arriving from Africa by the Via Appia would see the emperor's palace first. Three storeys of coloured-marble columns over three apsidal exedrae, about 90 m long; part survived until Sixtus V demolished it in 1588-1589.

phases.t: dedicated (CIL VI 1032)

scholarship: Richardson (1992) 350-351
Claridge, Rome (2010) 147
Lusnia, 'Urban planning and sculptural display in Severan Rome: reconstructing the Septizodium', AJA 108 (2004)
b:septizodium_v1.note: Position at the corner of Via dei Cerchi and Via di S. Gregorio (Wikipedia 41.8854, 12.4889; foundations seen in 2010s). Facade bearing ~150 (SSE, toward the Via Appia and Porta Capena) is inferred from its purpose and FUR fragment 8; height ~32 m estimated from Renaissance drawings of the surviving three-storey section.

b:baths_of_caracalla_v1.summary: Begun by Septimius Severus and dedicated by Caracalla in 216: a symmetrical bath block 214 x 110 m with the cold pool (natatio), the vaulted frigidarium hall and the domed caldarium on the main axis, twin palaestrae at the sides, and room for about 1,600 bathers. The outer enclosure was still unfinished.

phases.t: construction under way after Geta's murder
dedicated by Caracalla

scholarship: DeLaine, The Baths of Caracalla (JRA Suppl. 25, 1997)
Richardson (1992) 387-389
Claridge, Rome (2010) 359-365
b:baths_of_caracalla_v1.note: Precinct centre from the OSM site outline (axis 134/44 deg); bath block offset ~25 m NE of precinct centre; main entrances on the NE side toward the Via Nova, hence rot 44. Caldarium dome ~36 m span, ~44 m to the top (DeLaine).

b:baths_of_caracalla_v2.summary: The enclosure (peribolos) of 337 x 328 m was completed under Elagabalus and Severus Alexander: shops on the street front, two great exedrae with halls on the flanks, libraries and the stepped stadium-seating facing a running track over the vast cisterns on the SW side. Fed by the Aqua Antoniniana branch of the Marcia. Restored under Aurelian and by Theodoric, it worked until the Goths cut the aqueducts in 537.

phases.t: porticoes of the enclosure finished (HA Elag. 17.8-9; Alex. Sev. 25.6)
repairs under Aurelian
Theodoric restores the baths (Cassiodorus Var. 3.31)

scholarship: DeLaine (1997)
Richardson (1992) 387-389
b:baths_of_caracalla_v2.note: Precinct footprint from DeLaine; height of precinct ranges 10-14 m.

b:baths_of_caracalla_v3.summary: When Vitiges' Goths cut the aqueducts in 537 the baths went dry for good; the shell stood, roofs failing over the following centuries.
scholarship: DeLaine (1997)

b:temple_of_honos_et_virtus_v1.summary: M. Claudius Marcellus, conqueror of Syracuse, rebuilt an older temple of Honos outside the Porta Capena as twin shrines of Honour and Virtue, filled with Syracusan art; his son dedicated it in 205.
scholarship: Richardson (1992) 190
b:temple_of_honos_et_virtus_v1.note: Outside the Porta Capena by the Via Appia, facing the road toward the city (NW); site unknown.

b:temple_of_honos_et_virtus_v2.summary: Restored by Vespasian, whose painters Cornelius Pinus and Attius Priscus decorated it.
scholarship: Richardson (1992) 190

b:temple_of_tempestates_v1.summary: Vowed by L. Cornelius Scipio after his fleet escaped a storm off Corsica in 259 BC, as his epitaph in the Tomb of the Scipios records; near the Porta Capena.
scholarship: Richardson (1992) 378
b:temple_of_tempestates_v1.note: Placed by the Via Appia between Porta Capena and the Scipio tomb.

b:temple_of_mars_via_appia_v1.summary: Temple of Mars between the first and second milestones of the Via Appia, vowed in the Gallic war and dedicated in 388 BC; the army assembled here before marching south, and the Transvectio equitum set out from it on 15 July. The road leading to it was paved in 296 BC.
scholarship: Richardson (1992) 244-245
b:temple_of_mars_via_appia_v1.note: Commonly placed just outside the later Porta Appia near the Almo crossing; position conjectural.

b:tomb_of_the_scipios_v1.summary: Family tomb of the Cornelii Scipiones cut into the tufa on a side road between the Via Appia and Via Latina; the first burial is L. Cornelius Scipio Barbatus (consul 298), whose peperino sarcophagus is now in the Vatican.
scholarship: Coarelli, 'Il sepolcro degli Scipioni', Dialoghi di Archeologia 6 (1972) 36-106
Richardson (1992) 359-360
b:tomb_of_the_scipios_v1.note: Centre from OSM (Sepolcro degli Scipioni); the facade faced NW onto the side road (Coarelli).

b:tomb_of_the_scipios_v2.summary: Around the mid-second century, probably under Scipio Aemilianus, a second chamber was cut and a painted facade added: a rusticated podium with an arched entrance and an upper storey of half-columns framing three niches with statues of Africanus, Asiaticus and the poet Ennius. Burials continued into the first century AD; in the third century a house was built over it.
scholarship: Coarelli (1972)
Claridge, Rome (2010) 375-377

b:columbarium_pomponius_hylas_v1.summary: Small underground columbarium of the early first century AD near the Porta Latina, with a mosaic panel naming Pomponius Hylas and Pomponia Vitalinis and some of the best preserved stucco and painting of any Roman columbarium.
scholarship: Claridge, Rome (2010) 377-378
Richardson (1992) 93
b:columbarium_pomponius_hylas_v1.note: Centre from OSM; mostly below ground, entrance stair to the SW assumed.

b:columbarium_vigna_codini_1_v1.summary: One of three sunken columbaria in the former Vigna Codini between the Via Appia and Via Latina, for the freedmen and slaves of the Julio-Claudian household (some 500 niches).
scholarship: Richardson (1992) 93
Claridge, Rome (2010) 378
b:columbarium_vigna_codini_1_v1.note: Positions of the three columbaria within the vineyard approximate (about 80 m S of the Pomponius Hylas columbarium).

b:columbarium_vigna_codini_2_v1.summary: One of three sunken columbaria in the former Vigna Codini between the Via Appia and Via Latina, for the freedmen and slaves of the Julio-Claudian household (some 450 niches).
scholarship: Richardson (1992) 93
Claridge, Rome (2010) 378
b:columbarium_vigna_codini_2_v1.note: Positions of the three columbaria within the vineyard approximate (about 80 m S of the Pomponius Hylas columbarium).

b:columbarium_vigna_codini_3_v1.summary: One of three sunken columbaria in the former Vigna Codini between the Via Appia and Via Latina, for the freedmen and slaves of the Julio-Claudian household (some 300 niches).
scholarship: Richardson (1992) 93
Claridge, Rome (2010) 378
b:columbarium_vigna_codini_3_v1.note: Positions of the three columbaria within the vineyard approximate (about 80 m S of the Pomponius Hylas columbarium).

b:arch_of_drusus_v1.summary: Arch carrying the Aqua Antoniniana, the branch of the Marcia built for the Baths of Caracalla, across the Via Appia, decorated with columns of giallo antico; in the Renaissance wrongly named after Drusus. From 271 it stood just inside the Porta Appia.
scholarship: Richardson (1992) 23
Claridge, Rome (2010) 379
b:arch_of_drusus_v1.note: Footprint 11 x 5.1 m from OSM; the road passes through it on a bearing ~348/168. Attic carried the specus.

b:tomb_of_caecilia_metella_v1.summary: The great drum tomb of Caecilia Metella, daughter of Q. Metellus Creticus and daughter-in-law of Crassus, at the third milestone of the Via Appia: a travertine-faced cylinder 29.5 m across on a square base, with a frieze of ox-skulls and garlands that gave the area its name Capo di Bove.
scholarship: Richardson (1992) 353
Gerding, The Tomb of Caecilia Metella (2002)
b:tomb_of_caecilia_metella_v1.note: Centre from OSM. Inscription faces the road (SW); the road runs at bearing ~132 here. The medieval battlements are post-641.

b:circus_of_maxentius_v1.summary: The best-preserved Roman circus, built by Maxentius beside his villa and his son Romulus' mausoleum on the Via Appia: about 513 x 92 m with twelve carceres between two towers, a spina carrying the obelisk Domitian had made (now in Piazza Navona), and about 10,000 seats. It may have been used only for the inaugural games before Maxentius fell in 312.
scholarship: Pisani Sartorio and Calza, La villa di Massenzio sulla Via Appia (1976)
b:circus_of_maxentius_v1.note: Centre and axis (93/273) from OSM; carceres at the western end toward the Via Appia, curved end east, so rot 273.

b:mausoleum_of_romulus_v1.summary: Rotunda with a pronaos like a small Pantheon, inside a quadriporticus 107 x 121 m fronting the Via Appia, probably built by Maxentius for his son Valerius Romulus, who died in 309. The circular crypt with a central pier survives below a later farmhouse.
scholarship: Pisani Sartorio and Calza (1976)
Johnson, The Roman Imperial Mausoleum in Late Antiquity (2009) 86-93
b:mausoleum_of_romulus_v1.note: Centre from OSM (Mausoleo di Romolo). The complex lies NE of the Via Appia and faces it (SW, rot 222).

b:villa_of_maxentius_palace_v1.summary: Maxentius rebuilt an older villa on the hill north of the circus as a residence with an apsed audience hall (aula) and a long portico linking it to the imperial box of the circus.
scholarship: Pisani Sartorio and Calza (1976)
De Franceschini, Ville dell'Agro Romano (2005)
b:villa_of_maxentius_palace_v1.note: Position and layout approximate from published plans; the villa occupies the rise between the circus and the Via Appia Pignatelli.

b:tomb_of_priscilla_v1.summary: Drum tomb on a square base built by Domitian's freedman T. Flavius Abascantus for his wife Priscilla, near the fork of the Via Appia and Via Ardeatina; Statius describes its statues of the deceased as Ceres, Ariadne, Maia and Venus.
scholarship: Richardson (1992) 357
b:tomb_of_priscilla_v1.note: Coordinates approximate (Via Appia at the Quo Vadis fork); not matched in OSM. Inside the model bbox, so included although the brief marked it as possibly out of range.

b:emporium_quay_v1.summary: When the old river harbour by the Forum Boarium grew too small, the aediles M. Aemilius Lepidus and L. Aemilius Paullus laid out a new Emporium on the open plain south of the Aventine in 193 BC, about 500 m of river front.
scholarship: Richardson (1992) 143
Mocchegiani Carpano, 'Indagini archeologiche nel Tevere', Archeologia Laziale 2 (1979)
Coarelli, Rome and Environs (2007) 355-358
b:emporium_quay_v1.note: Line along the left bank following the excavated quay remains on Lungotevere Testaccio (OSM 'Emporium' site, bank bearing 46/226 deg), extended to ~500 m. rot faces the river (NW).

b:emporium_quay_v2.summary: The censors Q. Fulvius Flaccus and A. Postumius Albinus paved the Emporium in stone, fenced it and built stairs down to the river.
scholarship: Richardson (1992) 143
Mocchegiani Carpano, 'Indagini archeologiche nel Tevere', Archeologia Laziale 2 (1979)
Coarelli, Rome and Environs (2007) 355-358

b:emporium_quay_v3.summary: Rebuilt in the late first and early second centuries as a brick-faced embankment with travertine mooring blocks, ramps and stairs, behind which marble blocks, wine, oil and grain were unloaded for the warehouses of the Testaccio plain. The visible stretch on Lungotevere Testaccio belongs to this phase.
scholarship: Richardson (1992) 143
Mocchegiani Carpano, 'Indagini archeologiche nel Tevere', Archeologia Laziale 2 (1979)
Coarelli, Rome and Environs (2007) 355-358
b:emporium_quay_v3.note: Height above the low river level about 6 m.

b:porticus_aemilia_v1.summary: Built by the same aediles as the Emporium in 193 BC 'extra portam Trigeminam' as the great covered hall behind the new port.
scholarship: Richardson (1992) 311
Cozza and Tucci, 'Navalia', Archeologia Classica 57 (2006) 175-202
Arata and Felici, 'Porticus Aemilia, navalia o horrea?', Archeologia Classica 62 (2011)
Rodriguez Almeida, Forma Urbis Marmorea (1981) pl. 23
b:porticus_aemilia_v1.note: Livy says it was rebuilt in 174 BC; the surviving opus incertum structure is usually assigned to that phase.

b:porticus_aemilia_v2.summary: A colossal hall 487 x 60 m of opus incertum concrete, its 294 piers carrying 50 parallel barrel-vaulted aisles that stepped down the slope toward the Tiber, the earliest large concrete building in Rome. It appears on the Severan Marble Plan inscribed ...]LIA. Traditionally the Porticus Aemilia warehouse of the Emporium; Cozza and Tucci (2006) identified it instead as the Navalia, the shipsheds of the Republican fleet, an identification still debated.

phases.t: rebuilt by the censors Q. Fulvius Flaccus and A. Postumius Albinus (Livy 41.27.8)
used and partly rebuilt as warehouses in the Empire

scholarship: Richardson (1992) 311
Cozza and Tucci, 'Navalia', Archeologia Classica 57 (2006) 175-202
Arata and Felici, 'Porticus Aemilia, navalia o horrea?', Archeologia Classica 62 (2011)
Rodriguez Almeida, Forma Urbis Marmorea (1981) pl. 23
b:porticus_aemilia_v2.note: Centre and long-axis bearing (46.7 deg) from OSM (Porticus Aemilia remains, Via Rubattino/Via Branca); front faces the river (NW, 316.7). Aisles run perpendicular to the river; 50 aisles x ~8.3 m plus walls. The excavated segment is near the middle of the length.

b:horrea_galbana_v1.summary: Warehouses of the Sulpicii Galbae behind the Emporium, probably built by Ser. Sulpicius Galba (consul 108 BC), whose tomb stood among them.
scholarship: Richardson (1992) 193
Rickman, Roman Granaries and Store Buildings (1971) 97-104
b:horrea_galbana_v1.note: Dates of the Republican phase approximate.

b:horrea_galbana_v2.summary: Taken into imperial ownership under Galba and rebuilt: three long courtyards surrounded by about 140 storerooms in two storeys, shown on the Marble Plan as HORREA GALBIANA. A main store for oil, wine, foodstuffs and goods for the city; still listed in the fourth-century Regionary Catalogues.
scholarship: Richardson (1992) 193
Rodriguez Almeida, Forma Urbis Marmorea (1981)
b:horrea_galbana_v2.note: Placed east of the Porticus Aemilia between Via Marmorata and Via Galvani as on Lanciani's FUR; same alignment as the Porticus.

b:tomb_of_servius_sulpicius_galba_v1.summary: Altar-shaped tomb of Ser. Sulpicius Galba (consul 108 BC) found in 1885 at Via Giovanni Branca within the Horrea Galbana area; its inscription is in the Vatican.
scholarship: Richardson (1992) 359

b:horrea_lolliana_v1.summary: Warehouses originally of the Lollii (perhaps M. Lollius, consul 21 BC), later imperial, shown on the Marble Plan as HORREA LOLLIANA near the river; a gate with the name's inscription survived near the Emporium.
scholarship: Richardson (1992) 195
b:horrea_lolliana_v1.note: Usually placed on the riverside north of the Porticus Aemilia, behind the Emporium; date of foundation uncertain.

b:horrea_seiana_v1.summary: Warehouses named after the family of Seius Strabo and Sejanus, attested by inscriptions found in the Testaccio area near the Horrea Galbana.
scholarship: Richardson (1992) 196

b:monte_testaccio_v1.summary: Dumping of broken oil amphorae from the Emporium's unloading begins on the open ground east of the river, forming a low heap.

phases.t: height about 3 m

scholarship: Blazquez Martinez and Remesal Rodriguez, Estudios sobre el Monte Testaccio (1999-2019)

b:monte_testaccio_v2.summary: Through the first century the heap of sherds grows in deliberately terraced dumps, the empty amphorae being smashed and the pieces stacked, sprinkled with lime against the smell of rancid oil.

b:pyramid_of_cestius_v1.summary: Tomb of the praetor, tribune and septemvir epulonum C. Cestius Epulo, finished within 330 days according to its inscription: a pyramid 100 Roman feet square and 125 high, of concrete faced with white Luna marble, with a small painted burial chamber. It stood by the Via Ostiensis among other tombs, with two columns and statues at its corners.

phases.t: completed by the heirs, including Agrippa (CIL VI 1374-1375)

scholarship: Richardson (1992) 353
Claridge, Rome (2010) 400-402
Ridley, 'The pyramid of Gaius Cestius', in Ancient Society 23 (1992)
b:pyramid_of_cestius_v1.note: Centre and alignment (sides at 24/114 deg) from OSM. rot 114 = the inscribed east face toward the Via Ostiensis.

b:pyramid_of_cestius_v2.summary: Aurelian's builders incorporated the pyramid into the city wall as a bastion next to the Porta Ostiensis, which saved it.
scholarship: Richardson (1992) 353
Claridge, Rome (2010) 400-402
Ridley, 'The pyramid of Gaius Cestius', in Ancient Society 23 (1992)
b:pyramid_of_cestius_v2.note: Same structure; new version for the change of setting (wall built against its flanks).

b:porticus_sancti_pauli_v1.summary: A roofed colonnade some 2 km long that sheltered pilgrims on the road from the Porta Ostiensis to the basilica of St Paul, built around 400; Procopius mentions it during the siege of 537.
scholarship: Krautheimer, Rome: Profile of a City (1980) 24
Brandenburg, Ancient Churches of Rome (2005) 114-130
b:porticus_sancti_pauli_v1.note: Line follows the modern Via Ostiense, which keeps the ancient course; date approximate.

b:necropolis_via_ostiensis_v1.summary: Tombs of the late Republic to the fourth century lining the Via Ostiensis south of the Porta Ostiensis, excavated near the Centrale Montemartini; the cemetery around Paul's grave lay further south.
scholarship: Lugli, 'La necropoli Ostiense', Notizie degli Scavi (1919)
b:necropolis_via_ostiensis_v1.note: Generic tomb cluster at the excavated stretch along Via Ostiense; individual tombs schematic.

b:san_paolo_fuori_le_mura_v1.summary: A modest basilica built under Constantine over the tomb of the apostle Paul on the Via Ostiensis, its apse to the west at the grave and its entrance facing the road to the east; part of its apse was found in 1850 under the later transept.
scholarship: Krautheimer, Corpus Basilicarum Christianarum Romae V (1977) 93-164
Brandenburg, Ancient Churches of Rome (2005) 114-130
Filippi, excavations at the tomb of St Paul (2002-2006)
b:san_paolo_fuori_le_mura_v1.note: Placed ~75 m east of the present basilica's centroid, east of the tomb under the transept, entrance to the east (rot 100.7). Dimensions approximate.

b:san_paolo_fuori_le_mura_v2.summary: In 386 Valentinian II, Theodosius and Arcadius ordered a basilica to rival St Peter's; to make room the axis was reversed, so the new church faced west toward the Tiber with its apse to the east over Paul's tomb. Five aisles divided by 80 columns, a nave 24.6 m wide and about 30 m high, a transept and a colonnaded atrium: 128 m long and 65 m wide. Completed under Honorius; restored and decorated by Galla Placidia and Leo I. It stood intact until the fire of 1823 and was rebuilt on the same plan.

phases.t: imperial rescript to the urban prefect Sallustius (Coll. Avell. 3)
completed under Honorius
mosaic of the triumphal arch, Galla Placidia and Leo I

scholarship: Krautheimer, Corpus V (1977) 93-164
Brandenburg (2005) 114-130
Krautheimer, Rome: Profile of a City (1980) 42-44
b:san_paolo_fuori_le_mura_v2.note: Centre and axis from OSM outline of the present basilica, rebuilt 1823-1854 on the ancient plan; facade faces west (rot 280.7) toward the quadriporticus and the river.

b:naumachia_augusti_v1.summary: Augustus dug a basin 1,800 by 1,200 Roman feet (about 536 x 357 m) across the Tiber for a staged naval battle of Athenians and Persians at the dedication of Mars Ultor in 2 BC: thirty beaked ships and 3,000 fighters. Fed by the new Aqua Alsietina, it had an island reached by a bridge and was surrounded by the grove of the Caesars. Titus staged battles in it again in 80.

phases.t: naval battle for the dedication of the Temple of Mars Ultor
Titus' naval shows (Dio 66.25.3)

scholarship: Taylor, 'Torrent or trickle? The Aqua Alsietina, the Naumachia Augusti, and the Transtiberim', AJA 101 (1997) 465-492
Richardson (1992) 265
Liberati, LTUR III (1996) 337
b:naumachia_augusti_v1.note: No remains found. Placed near S. Cosimato between S. Maria in Trastevere, S. Francesco a Ripa and the river (Taylor), long axis assumed NNW-SSE (340/160) parallel to the river; position, orientation and end date all conjectural (out of use by the 3rd century).

b:nemus_caesarum_v1.summary: With the basin drained and partly built over, the area of the naumachia survived as gardens and scattered building; the name Naumachia still clung to the district in the Middle Ages.
scholarship: Taylor (1997)

b:horti_caesaris_pavilion_v1.summary: Caesar's suburban gardens on the right bank along the Via Portuensis, where Cleopatra stayed in 46-44 BC; Caesar left them to the Roman people in his will. A residential pavilion facing the river is modelled here.
scholarship: Richardson (1992) 200
Papi, LTUR III (1996) 55-56
b:horti_caesaris_pavilion_v1.note: The gardens' extent (see gardens collection) lay south of Porta Portese near the first milestone of the Via Portuensis; buildings unknown.

b:temple_of_fors_fortuna_v1.summary: Sp. Carvilius built a temple of Fors Fortuna near the old Servian shrine at the first milestone of the Via Portuensis from the spoils of the Samnite war (293 BC). On 24 June the people sailed down the river in garlanded boats to her festival.
scholarship: Richardson (1992) 154-155
b:temple_of_fors_fortuna_v1.note: Site in the Horti Caesaris area, position conjectural.

b:temple_of_fors_fortuna_v2.summary: Tiberius dedicated a temple of Fors Fortuna in the Gardens of Caesar in AD 16 near the Tiber, from Germanicus' victories.
scholarship: Richardson (1992) 155
b:temple_of_fors_fortuna_v2.note: Treated as the successor on the same site; the sources may refer to a separate building.

b:lucus_furrinae_v1.summary: Sacred grove and spring of the old goddess Furrina on the slope of the Janiculum, where Gaius Gracchus had himself killed by his slave in 121 BC.
scholarship: Goddard, 'The Syrian sanctuary on the Janiculum', in Papers of the British School at Rome 76 (2008)
Calzini Gysens and Duthoy, LTUR III (1996) 138-143
Richardson (1992) 223
b:lucus_furrinae_v1.note: Location at the springs below Villa Sciarra (Via Dandolo) where dedications to the Nymphae Furrinae were found.

b:syrian_sanctuary_janiculum_v1.summary: In the second century merchants and devotees of Syrian gods, notably the Syrian M. Antonius Gaionas, built a sanctuary of Jupiter Heliopolitanus (Hadad) and the Nymphs of Furrina around the spring, known from dedications of about 176.
scholarship: Goddard, 'The Syrian sanctuary on the Janiculum', in Papers of the British School at Rome 76 (2008)
Calzini Gysens and Duthoy, LTUR III (1996) 138-143
Richardson (1992) 223

b:syrian_sanctuary_janiculum_v2.summary: Rebuilt in the fourth century as a three-part building on an east-west axis: a western basilical hall with an apse, a central court, and an eastern octagonal room with a triangular altar under which a bronze statuette of a god wrapped by a serpent and eggs were buried; a late pagan cult centre abandoned around 400.
scholarship: Goddard, 'The Syrian sanctuary on the Janiculum', in Papers of the British School at Rome 76 (2008)
Calzini Gysens and Duthoy, LTUR III (1996) 138-143
Richardson (1992) 223
b:syrian_sanctuary_janiculum_v2.note: Plan from Gauckler's excavation; the entrance was on the east side (rot 90) with the basilical sanctuary to the west.

b:janiculum_mills_v1.summary: Flour mills driven by the outflow of the Aqua Traiana as it ran down the Janiculum slope, a chain of millhouses on a stepped millrace. Excavated under the American Academy and Via Garibaldi; the excavated mill phases run from the early third century to the sixth. They ground the city's bread until Vitiges cut the aqueduct in 537, when Belisarius moved the mills onto boats in the Tiber.

phases.t: Aqua Traiana opened (109); mills along its terminal run
law protecting the Janiculum mills (CTh 14.15.4)

scholarship: Wilson, 'The water-mills on the Janiculum', MAAR 45 (2000) 219-246
Bell, 'An archaeologist's revenge', in Archeologia Laziale 12 (1995)
b:janiculum_mills_v1.note: Line of mills along the course of the aqueduct inside the Aurelian Wall near Porta Aurelia; dated here from the aqueduct (109) as the brief calls them Trajanic, though the excavated mills are early third century onward.

b:janiculum_mills_v2.summary: Idle after the Goths cut the aqueduct in 537; later restorations of the Traiana (7th-8th century) may have revived some.
scholarship: Wilson (2000)

b:villa_farnesina_roman_v1.summary: Luxurious riverside villa of the early Augustan age, probably of Agrippa and Julia, found in 1879 while building the Tiber embankment: a great hemicycle corridor facing the river and rooms with famous Third Style paintings and stuccoes, now in the Palazzo Massimo.
scholarship: Bragantini and de Vos, Le decorazioni della villa romana della Farnesina (1982)
Richardson (1992) 425
b:villa_farnesina_roman_v1.note: Excavated under the Lungotevere east of Villa Farnesina and destroyed by the embankment; position approximate. The hemicycle faced the river (SE).

b:castra_ravennatium_v1.summary: Barracks of the detachment of the Ravenna fleet stationed in Rome, listed in Regio XIV; the marines worked the awnings and the naval shows.
scholarship: Richardson (1992) 78
b:castra_ravennatium_v1.note: Placed near S. Callisto / S. Maria in Trastevere where it is usually located; plan generic.

b:tiber_island_ship_v1.summary: In the first century BC the downstream end of the island was faced with travertine blocks carved as the prow of a ship, recalling the vessel that brought Aesculapius' serpent from Epidaurus; an obelisk in the middle served as mast. A section with the bust of the god and his staff survives at the SE point.
scholarship: Richardson (1992) 209
Claridge, Rome (2010) 252-253
b:tiber_island_ship_v1.note: Island centre and axis (111.7 deg) from OSM; length 270 m, width 67 m. rot = bow bearing, downstream (ESE). Date approximate, often linked to the Pons Fabricius (62 BC).

b:temple_of_aesculapius_v1.summary: After a plague in 293 BC an embassy brought the sacred serpent of Asclepius from Epidaurus; it slipped ashore on the island, where the temple was dedicated on 1 January 291. Porticoes around it served as a sanatorium where the sick slept for healing dreams; Claudius ruled that slaves abandoned there became free.

phases.t: dedication (Livy Per. 11)
Claudius' edict on abandoned sick slaves (Suet. Claud. 25.2)

scholarship: Richardson (1992) 3
Degrassi, LTUR I (1993) 21-22

b:obelisk_tiber_island_v1.summary: A small obelisk set in the middle of the island as the 'mast' of the stone ship; fragments are in Naples and Munich, and its place is marked by the column in Piazza di S. Bartolomeo.
scholarship: Richardson (1992) 209
D'Onofrio, Gli obelischi di Roma (1992)

b:temple_of_faunus_island_v1.summary: Built by the plebeian aediles Cn. Domitius Ahenobarbus and C. Scribonius Curio from fines on graziers, dedicated in 194 BC at the upstream end of the island; Vitruvius cites it with its neighbour as prostyle.
scholarship: Richardson (1992) 209-210
Degrassi, LTUR (1993-2000) s.v.

b:temple_of_veiovis_island_v1.summary: Vowed by L. Furius Purpureo in 200 BC in Cisalpine Gaul and dedicated in 194 BC on the island; Vitruvius pairs it with the temple of Faunus as prostyle.
scholarship: Richardson (1992) 209-210
Degrassi, LTUR (1993-2000) s.v.

scholarship: Richardson (1992) 209-210
Degrassi, LTUR (1993-2000) s.v.

scholarship: Richardson (1992) 209-210
Degrassi, LTUR (1993-2000) s.v.
b:shrine_of_iuppiter_iurarius_v1.note: Located by the mosaic found at S. Giovanni Calibita (OSM).

b:shrine_of_semo_sancus_island_v1.summary: A shrine of Semo Sancus on the island, known from the base dedicated 'Semoni Sanco deo fidio' found in 1574, which early Christian writers misread as a statue of Simon Magus.
scholarship: Richardson (1992) 209-210
Degrassi, LTUR (1993-2000) s.v.
b:shrine_of_semo_sancus_island_v1.note: Find-spot near S. Bartolomeo; form conjectural.

b:circus_of_gaius_and_nero_v1.summary: Private circus laid out by Caligula in the gardens of his mother Agrippina on the Vatican plain, with a 25.5 m obelisk from Heliopolis (dedicated by Cornelius Gallus, rededicated to Augustus and Tiberius) on its spina. Nero raced here and in 64 had Christians put to death in it and in the gardens; tradition places Peter's martyrdom here.

phases.t: obelisk brought from Alexandria in a giant ship (Pliny 16.201)
Christians executed in Nero's gardens and circus (Tac. Ann. 15.44)

scholarship: Liverani, La topografia antica del Vaticano (1999)
Castagnoli, Il Vaticano nell'antichita classica (1992)
Humphrey, Roman Circuses (1986) 545-552
b:circus_of_gaius_and_nero_v1.note: Axis parallel to Old St Peter's, whose south wall rested on the circus' north side; curved end west, carceres east (rot 90). Length ~540 m after the brief; Castagnoli and Liverani reconstruct 500-560 m. The obelisk stood at the plaque in Piazza dei Protomartiri Romani, ~149 m west of the assumed centre.

b:circus_of_gaius_and_nero_v2.summary: By the second and third centuries tombs encroached on the circus, which went out of use; its north side was buried under the terrace of Old St Peter's from 319. The obelisk stayed standing on the spina line until Sixtus V moved it to Piazza San Pietro in 1586.
scholarship: Liverani, La topografia antica del Vaticano (1999)
Castagnoli, Il Vaticano nell'antichita classica (1992)

b:vatican_necropolis_v1.summary: Two rows of brick house-tombs of the second and early third centuries lining a lane on the Vatican slope north of the circus, belonging to well-off freedman families (Caetennii, Valerii, Julii with the Christ-Helios mosaic). Excavated 1940-1949 under the Vatican basilica.
scholarship: Toynbee and Ward-Perkins, The Shrine of St Peter and the Vatican Excavations (1956)
Liverani and Spinola, The Vatican Necropoles (2010)
b:vatican_necropolis_v1.note: The lane ran east-west under the nave of the basilica, east of the tomb of Peter; the local frame uses rot 180 so the rows run along the E-W axis. Buried when Constantine's builders levelled the slope in 319-322.

b:tropaion_of_gaius_v1.summary: Around 160 a small two-storey niche with a travertine slab on two marble colonnettes was set against the 'Red Wall' of Campo P over a simple grave revered as Peter's; the priest Gaius named it 'the trophy' of the apostle around 200.
scholarship: Toynbee and Ward-Perkins (1956) 135-167
Liverani and Spinola (2010)
b:tropaion_of_gaius_v1.note: At the papal altar under the dome (St Peter's tomb location); faces east.

b:tropaion_of_gaius_v2.summary: Constantine encased the aedicula in a marble and porphyry box under a canopy of twisted vine-scroll columns at the chord of the apse, the focus of the new basilica; Gregory the Great raised the floor around it to make a crypt.
scholarship: Toynbee and Ward-Perkins (1956) 195-210
Krautheimer, Corpus V (1977) 165-279

b:old_st_peters_v1.summary: Constantine built the funerary basilica over Peter's grave from about 319, cutting into the Vatican hill and burying the necropolis on a vast terrace. Five aisles separated by 88 reused columns, a nave about 90 m long, a continuous transept with the shrine at the chord of the apse: about 119 m from apse to facade and 64 m wide. Occidented: the apse west, the entrance facing east toward the city.

phases.t: construction begins (dendro/coin evidence c. 319-322)
transept and apse in use

scholarship: Krautheimer, Corpus Basilicarum Christianarum Romae V (1977) 165-279
Westall, 'Constantius II and the basilica of St Peter', Historia 64 (2015)
Brandenburg, Ancient Churches of Rome (2005) 91-102
b:old_st_peters_v1.note: Apse chord at Peter's tomb (under the present dome, OSM); axis from the present basilica (89.4 deg); centre 47.5 m east of the tomb. Alfarano's plan (1571) gives the dimensions.

b:old_st_peters_v2.summary: Finished under Constantius II around 360 with the nave and the colonnaded atrium (the 'Paradise') in front of the facade, where Pope Symmachus later set the bronze pinecone fountain. The richest shrine of the West: the Goths spared it in 410, Leo I and Symmachus embellished it, and around it grew mausolea, monasteries and hostels.

phases.t: completed (dedicatory inscription of Constantius II)
Symmachus: atrium fountain, stairs, episcopia (LP 53)

scholarship: Krautheimer, Corpus V (1977) 165-279
Westall (2015)
b:old_st_peters_v2.note: Church l=119 excludes the atrium (~56 x 62 m east of the facade).

b:vatican_rotunda_v1.summary: A brick rotunda with eight niches built on the line of the old circus spina, probably a third-century imperial-class mausoleum; it appears on a third-century gem and was drawn before its demolition in 1776.
scholarship: Johnson, The Roman Imperial Mausoleum in Late Antiquity (2009) 167-174
b:vatican_rotunda_v1.note: Positions of the two rotundas south of the basilica's south transept from Alfarano's plan; the obelisk stood just south of this one. Entrance assumed on the north toward the basilica.

b:vatican_rotunda_v2.summary: Pope Symmachus (498-514) turned the rotunda into the church of St Andrew; later called S. Maria della Febbre, it served as the sacristy of St Peter's until 1776.
b:vatican_rotunda_v2.note: Conversion of an existing building; the brief assigns it here.

b:mausoleum_of_honorius_v1.summary: Dynastic mausoleum of the Theodosian house built against the south transept of St Peter's, entered from it through a vestibule. The empress Maria (died c. 407/408) and later probably Thermantia, Honorius himself (423) and members of Galla Placidia's family were buried here; Maria's sarcophagus with its jewels was found in 1544. Made a chapel of St Petronilla in 757; demolished 1519.
scholarship: Koethe, 'Das Mausoleum der Honorius', Jahrbuch des DAI 46 (1931)
b:mausoleum_of_honorius_v1.note: West of the Vatican Rotunda on the spina line, joined to the south arm of the transept; faces north (rot 0) into the basilica. Size similar to the Vatican Rotunda per the Anonimo Fiorentino plan.

b:phrygianum_v1.summary: Sanctuary of Cybele and Attis 'in Vaticano', where taurobolia were performed; altars dedicated by senators between 295 and 390 were found in 1609 under the facade of the new St Peter's, making it a stronghold of the last pagan aristocracy next door to the apostle's shrine.
scholarship: Liverani (1999) 25-27
Richardson (1992) 300
Roger Pearse, 'Old St Peter's, the Circus of Caligula and the Phrygianum' (2014)
b:phrygianum_v1.note: Location from the find-spot of the taurobolium altars near the facade of the present basilica; form unknown, a small precinct temple modelled. End date after the last dated altar (390) and the anti-pagan laws.

b:meta_romuli_v1.summary: A marble-faced pyramid tomb, larger than that of Cestius, at the junction of the Via Cornelia and Via Triumphalis, perhaps of Cornelius Gallus, prefect of Egypt; medieval Romans called it the tomb of Romulus. Pope Donus stripped its marble for the paving of St Peter's in the 670s; Alexander VI demolished it in 1499. Its foundations lie under the north side of Via della Conciliazione.
scholarship: Castagnoli (1992) 23-25
Platner-Ashby (1929) 340
Verzar-Bass, in Horti Romani (1998) 401-424
b:meta_romuli_v1.note: Coordinates from Wikipedia (foundations under the Auditorium della Conciliazione block); base 25 m square from 15th-century accounts, height 32-50 m, 40 used. Augustan date assumed.

b:terebinthus_neronis_v1.summary: A tall round tomb on a square base near the Meta Romuli, called the 'Terebinth of Nero' in medieval sources and shown in Filarete's bronze doors; demolished in the Middle Ages.
scholarship: Liverani (1999) 74-77
Castagnoli (1992) 25
b:terebinthus_neronis_v1.note: Position between the Meta Romuli and the Mausoleum of Hadrian conjectural; form from Filarete and Cimabue's views.

b:naumachia_vaticana_v1.summary: An artificial lake for naval battles with brick-built seating, dedicated by Trajan in 109 (Fasti Ostienses) and probably fed by the Aqua Traiana; its remains were seen in 1743 near Via Crescenzio and Piazza Cavour and in 1904.
scholarship: Richardson (1992) 266
b:naumachia_vaticana_v1.note: Extent and orientation approximate (long axis E-W ~300 m).

b:gaianum_v1.summary: An open training track for charioteers laid out by Caligula on the Vatican plain, still named in the Regionary Catalogues (Gaianum) and in Dio.
scholarship: Richardson (1992) 159
Liverani (1999) 116
b:gaianum_v1.note: Location in the plain between the Mausoleum of Hadrian and St Peter's (medieval Prata Neronis) conjectural.

b:necropolis_via_triumphalis_v1.summary: Terraced cemetery of slaves, freedmen and ordinary Romans along the Via Triumphalis on the Vatican hillside, with small tombs and columbaria of the late first century BC to the early fourth century AD; excavated 1956-2009 inside Vatican City.
scholarship: Steinby, La necropoli della Via Triumphalis (2003)
Liverani and Spinola (2010)
b:necropolis_via_triumphalis_v1.note: Cluster centred between the Autoparco and Santa Rosa sectors; schematic.

b:porticus_sancti_petri_v1.summary: A covered colonnade, the porticus maior, sheltering pilgrims from the Pons Aelius to the atrium of St Peter's, mentioned by Procopius in 537.
scholarship: Krautheimer, Rome: Profile of a City (1980) 24
Liverani (1999) 140
b:porticus_sancti_petri_v1.note: Course approximate along Via della Conciliazione/Borgo; construction date uncertain (5th century).

phases.t: First wall on the north slope (c. 730-720 BC): cappellaccio footings with a timber and clay superstructure, found by Carandini's excavations between the Arch of Titus and the House of the Vestals.
Rebuilt (second phase, c. 675 BC).
Third phase (c. 600 BC).
Fourth phase (c. 530 BC); aristocratic houses then line the Sacra Via against it.
No longer maintained; built over by the houses of the north slope. End date is a guess.

scholarship: Carandini and Carafa (eds.), The Atlas of Ancient Rome (2017) I, Palatine
Carandini, Remo e Romolo (2006)
w:palatine_archaic_wall.note: Only the north-slope stretch (c. 80 m, around [12.4870, 41.8910]) has been excavated; the full circuit around the foot of the hill is Carandini's hypothesis, partly modelled on the Palatine pomerium of Tacitus (Ann. 12.24) and drawn here a few metres inside the modern streets at the base (Via di S. Teodoro, Via dei Cerchi, Via di S. Gregorio). Its dating and even its function as a wall (rather than a pomerial boundary) are disputed.

phases.t: Cappellaccio walls round the cliff edges of the Capitolium and Arx (remains below the retaining wall above Vicolo della Rupe Tarpea and near the Aracoeli stairs).
The Capitol alone holds out against the Gauls; Manlius repulses the night assault on the Arx (Livy 5.47).
West side rebuilt as part of the Servian circuit in Grotta Oscura tufa.
South-east side masked by the substructures of the Tabularium and the Area Capitolina; the walls survive as retaining walls.

scholarship: Platner-Ashby 351 (remains on the north side of the Capitol)
Richardson, NTDAR (1992) 262-263
w:capitoline_fortifications.note: Drawn along the cliff edges of the two summits joined by the Asylum saddle. The western half coincides with the Servian line. East side (towards the Forum) conjectural; no city gate except the clivus entrances (Porta Pandana) is recorded.

phases.t: Tradition credits Servius Tullius (Livy 1.44.3; Dionysius 4.13): cappellaccio blocks (0.20-0.30 x 0.55-0.66 x 0.75-0.90 m) with an earth agger on the Esquiline plateau.
Gallic sack: the circuit fails to stop the Senones (Livy 5.38-41).
Replacement in Grotta Oscura tufa begins; old stretches incorporated or dismantled.

scholarship: Platner-Ashby 350-352
Cifani, Le mura serviane (various, 1998-2016)
Bernard, Building Mid-Republican Rome (2018)
w:servian_wall_archaic.note: Whether a complete 6th-century circuit existed is debated (Cifani; Fontaine vs. those who see only an agger and hilltop defences). Drawn on the same course as the 4th-century wall, which reused it in places (cappellaccio stretches survive at the agger and on the Aventine).

phases.t: Censors let the contract for a wall of squared stone (Livy 6.32.1); work in 30-40 m lots by separate gangs, possibly with Syracusan masons; Grotta Oscura tufa from the territory of conquered Veii.
Wall and towers repaired / completed (Livy 7.20.9). Height about 10 m, thickness about 4 m; agger and ditch across the Esquiline plateau.
After Trasimene the walls and towers are repaired (Livy 22.8.6).
Further repairs during the Hannibalic War; in 211 Hannibal rides up to the Porta Collina (Livy 26.10).

Bellum Octavianum: the circuit is refurbished for artillery, with arched catapult embrasures (viale Aventino stretch; the Palazzo Antonelli arch on the Quirinal is attributed to this work) (Appian, BC 1.66-69).
Battle of the Colline Gate (Sulla against the Samnites) outside the north-east corner.

No longer maintained under Augustus; houses press against both faces and the circuit becomes hard to trace (Dionysius 4.13.5); Maecenas lays gardens over the agger and Esquiline cemetery (Horace, Sat. 1.8.14-16).
The stretch across the Quirinal saddle disappears in the cutting for Trajan's Forum and Markets.
Stands only in fragments embedded in houses, horti and public buildings; gates survive as arches (Porta Esquilina rebuilt as the Arch of Gallienus in 262).
Remnants used as quarry and foundations; long stretches still visible on the agger and Aventine.

scholarship: Platner-Ashby 350-355
Säflund, Le mura di Roma repubblicana (1932)
Coarelli, Rome and Environs (2007) 14-17
Richardson, NTDAR (1992) 262-263
w:servian_wall.note: Course drawn through the surviving stretches and gate sites: Aracoeli and Capitoline foot, Largo Magnanapoli, Palazzo Colonna, Via della Dataria, Via delle Scuderie and Via dei Giardini, Largo S. Susanna, Via Salandra, Via Goito / Via XX Settembre (Porta Collina), the agger remains north of and in front of Termini and in the station, Piazza Manfredo Fanti, the Arch of Gallienus, Via Mecenate (Auditorium of Maecenas), Via Poliziano, S. Clemente, the Arch of Dolabella, Porta Capena, S. Balbina, viale Aventino / Piazza Albania, Via di Sant'Anselmo and the west cliff of the Aventine (S. Sabina). Between surviving pieces the line follows the hill edges; my trace measures about 8.3 km against the c. 11 km usually quoted, because real wall lines zig-zag along contours. The river section is unknown (Livy suggests the wall ran down from the Aventine to the Tiber leaving the port open).

phases.t: Front wall of Grotta Oscura blocks 4 m thick backed by an earth rampart about 30 m wide (Dionysius: 7 stadia long, 50 ft thick) and fronted by a ditch about 100 Roman feet (30-36 m) wide and 30 ft (9 m) deep. Porta Viminalis the only gate between the Collina and Esquilina.
The rampart becomes a promenade ('aggere in aprico spatiari', Horace Sat. 1.8.15); the ditch beyond is filled with the Esquiline dumps and gardens.
Rampart still visible; the ditch is built over.

scholarship: Platner-Ashby 354
Lanciani, Ruins and Excavations of Ancient Rome (1897) 67-71
w:servian_agger.note: Line from the Porta Collina (Via XX Settembre / Via Goito) to the Porta Esquilina (Arch of Gallienus). Rampart on the inner (west) side; ditch line offset 24 m outward (east) to its centre. Large stretches seen in the 1860s-1870s works for Termini and the Esquiline quarter; the 94 m stretch in Piazza dei Cinquecento stands to about 8 m.

phases.t: Aurelian orders the circuit after the Juthungian invasion of Italy; built fast by the city's collegia, incorporating existing structures (Castra Praetoria, Pyramid of Cestius, Amphitheatrum Castrense, aqueduct arches, the Horti walls of the Muro Torto, tombs and insulae).
Largely complete at Aurelian's death. Curtain about 6-8 m high over 2 m footings, 3.3-3.5 m thick, with a crenellated walkway; square towers every 100 Roman feet with a ballista chamber.
Finished under Probus (Zosimus 1.49).

Maxentius begins a refurbishment against Constantine: a ditch (fossa) is dug, some stretches and the Castra Praetoria walls are raised; the attribution of the upper gallery to Maxentius (Richmond) is now doubted.
Constantine disbands the praetorians and razes the camp walls facing the city; the outer camp walls stay in the circuit.

Honorius and Stilicho double the height (to roughly 15-16 m): a covered gallery with arrow slits is built on the old walkway and a new open, crenellated walkway on top; towers raised by a storey; most gates rebuilt in travertine, many reduced to one arch; dedicatory inscriptions of 401-402 at the Tiburtina, Praenestina-Labicana and Portuensis (CIL VI 1188-1190).
Works completed for Honorius' triumph of 403; the Mausoleum of Hadrian is turned into a bridgehead fortress.
24 August: Alaric's Goths enter by the Porta Salaria; the wall itself is not breached.
Mid-5th-century repairs under Valentinian III after earthquake damage (date and extent uncertain).
Vandal sack: Geiseric enters without siege.
Theoderic funds restorations (Cassiodorus, Variae 1.25, 2.34; brick stamps REGE THEODERICO).
Belisarius repairs the circuit, recuts the ditch and fits merlons with a lateral wing (Procopius 5.14.15); the Muro Torto is left as it was.
Siege by Witiges (March 537 - March 538): assaults at the Porta Salaria, Praenestina (Vivarium), Aurelia/Mausoleum and Flaminia; the Goths cut the aqueducts.
17 December: Totila enters through the Porta Asinaria (Isaurian guards' treachery) and pulls down about a third of the circuit (Procopius 7.22.6-7).
Spring: Belisarius reoccupies Rome and closes the breaches in 25 days with rubble laid dry or in clay, without new gates (Procopius 7.24.3-6).
Totila retakes Rome (the Isaurians open the Porta Ostiensis, January 550 in some reckonings) and restores the circuit to hold it (Procopius 7.36-37).
Narses takes the city after Busta Gallorum; the circuit stays in use, as rebuilt.

Todd, The Walls of Rome (1978)

w:aurelian_wall.note: Land circuit chained from the OpenStreetMap 'Mura Aureliane' relation (surviving stretches, simplified to about 3.5 m), from the Porta del Popolo clockwise past the Muro Torto (a retaining wall of the Horti Aciliorum/Pinciani reused), Porta Pinciana, Salaria, Nomentana, the Castra Praetoria salient, Porta Chiusa, Tiburtina, the Porta Maggiore aqueduct arches, the Amphitheatrum Castrense, Porta Asinaria, Metronia, Latina, Appia, Ardeatina, Ostiensis and the Pyramid, to the Tiber at Testaccio. The river walls are reconstructed on the Lungotevere roads, roughly on the old bank. The line is open: the river between Ponte Sisto and Testaccio was covered by the Trastevere salient (see aurelian_wall_trastevere). Lengths: about 16.7 km here plus 2.2 km in Trastevere, against the 19 km usually given.

Bezzi, about 450 m south of the later Porta Portese) along Via degli Orti di Trastevere and Piazza B. da Feltre, up Viale Glorioso and Via A. Masina to the Porta Aurelia (Porta S. Pancrazio) on the Janiculum summit, then down along Via di Porta S. Pancrazio and the surviving stretch through the Porta Settimiana to the river just north of Ponte Sisto. phases.t: Honorius turns the mausoleum into a fortress covering the Pons Aelius, its precinct wall rebuilt with corner towers and linked to the Porta Aurelia-Sancti Petri on the left bank (Procopius 5.22.12-13).
The garrison breaks up the statues of the mausoleum and hurls them at the Goths (Procopius 5.22.20-22).

scholarship: Richmond, The City Wall of Imperial Rome (1930) 22-25
w:mausoleum_hadrian_bridgehead.note: Modelled as a 124 m square enclosure around the 89 m drum base, aligned on the Pons Aelius axis (bearing 176). The exact form of the Honorian enclosure is not known; the bridge itself and the mausoleum belong to the buildings collection.

phases.t: Sejanus concentrates the praetorian cohorts in a walled camp of about 440 x 380 m with rounded corners (Tacitus, Ann. 4.2; Suetonius, Tib. 37); early brick walls about 4.7 m high with crenellations.
Besieged by the people in the riots against the praetorians (Herodian 7.11-12).
Raised and absorbed into the Aurelian Wall (continued as part of aurelian_wall from 275).

Platner-Ashby, Castra Praetoria
