phases.t: Built with the camp.
Left standing inside the new circuit.
Razed by Constantine after Milvian Bridge when he disbands the guard (Aurelius Victor, Caes. 40.25; Zosimus 2.17.2).

scholarship: Richardson, NTDAR (1992) 78-79
w:castra_praetoria_inner_walls.note: SW corner computed as NW + (SE - NE). Constantine's demolition removed the walls facing the city, leaving the outer ones in the Aurelian circuit.

phases.t: Temple of Jupiter Stator vowed at the gate (Livy 10.36.11).

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Porta Mugonia
Carandini (ed.), Atlas of Ancient Rome (2017)
g:porta_mugonia.note: Old gate of the Palatine at the summa Sacra Via by the temple of Jupiter Stator, where the Clivus Palatinus later climbed (Varro LL 5.164; Livy 1.12.3, Dionysius 2.50.3). Placed just SW of the Arch of Titus. End date arbitrary: the site was rebuilt after the fire of 64.

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Porta Romana
Richardson, NTDAR (1992) 311
g:porta_romanula.note: Palatine gate on the Velabrum side with steps down to the Nova Via by the sacellum of Volupia (Varro LL 5.164; 6.24); Platner places it a little south of S. Teodoro, at the foot of the Clivus Victoriae.

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Scalae Caci
g:scalae_caci_gate.note: The stair from the Forum Boarium up to the Germalus by the hut of Romulus; treated by Carandini as the third entrance of the archaic circuit. Stair remains near the Casa Romuli.

scholarship: Richardson, NTDAR (1992) 302
g:porta_pandana.note: Gate of the old Capitoline fortress, 'always open' (Festus; Varro LL 5.42 calls it Saturnia, from the old name of the hill); placed where the Clivus Capitolinus reached the hilltop. End date arbitrary.

phases.t: The 306 Fabii leave by the right-hand arch (Livy 2.49.8; Ovid Fasti 2.201-204).
Rebuilt with the Grotta Oscura circuit.

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Porta Carmentalis
Coarelli, Rome and Environs (2007) 15
Coarelli, Il Foro Boario (1988)
g:porta_carmentalis.note: At the SW foot of the Capitol by the shrine of Carmenta, at the west end of the Vicus Iugarius (near the modern Anagrafe, Via Petroselli). Two passages; the right-hand one (Porta Scelerata) shunned after the Fabii marched out to the Cremera in 477 BC. Probably the gate passed by triumphs if it is not identical with the Porta Triumphalis. Facing set by hand (gate at a corner of the circuit).

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Porta Triumphalis
Richardson, NTDAR (1992) 301-302
Coarelli, Il Foro Boario (1988) 363-414
Beard, The Roman Triumph (2007) 96-101
g:porta_triumphalis.note: Triumphal processions entered the city by the Porta Triumphalis (Cicero, In Pisonem 55; Suetonius, Aug. 100; Tacitus, Ann. 1.8). Theories: (1) a gate of the Servian Wall between the Carmentalis and the river near Sant'Omobono, used only for triumphs (placed here; the Italian Wikipedia list follows this); (2) one arch of the double Porta Carmentalis (Coarelli); (3) a free-standing ceremonial arch in the Campus Martius by the Circus Flaminius and Villa Publica (Haselberger; Richardson); (4) not a fixed structure at all. Point is illustrative only.

phases.t: Flood reaches the gate (Livy 35.9.3; 35.21.5).

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Porta Flumentana
Richardson, NTDAR (1992) 302
g:porta_flumentana.note: Gate toward the river between the temple of Portunus and the Tiber, where the road from the Pons Aemilius (Via Aurelia) entered; sometimes flooded (Livy 35.9.3). Whether it stood in a continuous wall is unknown.

phases.t: Porticus built from the gate to the Tiber (Livy 35.10.12).
Arch restored by the consuls (CIL VI 1385).

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Porta Trigemina
Richardson, NTDAR (1992) 310
Coarelli, Il Foro Boario (1988)
g:porta_trigemina.note: Triple gate at the NW foot of the Aventine between the Forum Boarium and the river, by the Salinae; start of the Via Ostiensis and the Clivus Publicius. The 3.30 m arch found in 1885 near S. Maria in Cosmedin was proposed for it but is rejected by Platner. Inside the city by Augustus; arch restored by Lentulus and Crispinus (AD 2).

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Porta Lavernalis
g:porta_lavernalis.note: Aventine gate named from the altar of Laverna, perhaps beneath Sant'Anselmo, leading to the Via Ostiensis (Varro LL 5.163).

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Porta Raudusculana
Coarelli, Rome and Environs (2007) 16
g:porta_raudusculana.note: Gate in the saddle between the two Aventine summits at Piazza Albania, said to have been bronze-clad (raudus); a road (Vicus Portae Raudusculanae) led from it to the Ostiensis. The Viale Aventino stretch with the 87 BC catapult arch is just east.

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Porta Naevia
Richardson, NTDAR (1992) 306
g:porta_naevia.note: Gate between S. Saba and S. Balbina at the southern corner of the Lesser Aventine, leading to the Via Ardeatina (Varro LL 5.163).

phases.t: Via Appia begun from the gate.
Footway paved from the gate to the temple of Mars (Livy 10.23.12).
Aqua Marcia carried over the gate.
Antoniniana branch to the Baths of Caracalla.

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Porta Capena
Richardson, NTDAR (1992) 301
g:porta_capena.note: Gate between the Caelian and the Aventine at the head of the Via Appia and Via Latina, between the Circus Maximus valley and Via delle Terme di Caracalla. The arcade of the Aqua Marcia (and later the Antonine branch) passed over it, so that it dripped ('madida Capena', Juvenal 3.11; Martial 3.47.1).

phases.t: Rebuilt as the Arch of Dolabella and Silanus (consuls of AD 10).
Arcus Neroniani built over it.

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Porta Caelimontana
Coarelli, Rome and Environs (2007) 205
g:porta_caelimontana.note: On the Caelian near S. Maria in Domnica; replaced in AD 10 by the travertine Arch of Dolabella and Silanus (CIL VI 1384), later used by Nero's branch of the Aqua Claudia (Arcus Neroniani). Faces roughly SE.

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Porta Querquetulana
g:porta_querquetulana.note: Gate named from an oak grove, probably near S. Clemente between the Caelian and Oppius, at the head of the road that became the Via Tusculana / Asinaria (Pliny NH 16.37).

phases.t: Sulla forces his way into the city here (Appian BC 1.58).
Rebuilt as the Arch of Gallienus and Salonina.

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Porta Esquilina
Coarelli, Rome and Environs (2007) 192
g:porta_esquilina.note: At the top of the Clivus Suburanus on Via di S. Vito, start of the Via Labicana, Praenestina and Tiburtina; outside lay the Esquiline necropolis and puticuli. In 262 the gate was rebuilt as the travertine Arch of Gallienus (single surviving bay of an original three; about 8.8 m high) dedicated by M. Aurelius Victor (CIL VI 1106).

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Porta Viminalis
Platner-Ashby 354
g:porta_viminalis.note: The only gate through the agger, in Piazza dei Cinquecento just north of the surviving stretch; reached by the Vicus Patricius and Vicus Collis Viminalis.

phases.t: Gauls defeated before the gate (Livy 7.11).
Hannibal rides up to the gate (Livy 26.10.3).
Battle of the Colline Gate: Sulla defeats the Samnites and Marians (1 November 82 BC).

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Porta Collina
Richardson, NTDAR (1992) 302
g:porta_collina.note: North-east corner of the circuit at the corner of Via XX Settembre and Via Goito (site of the Ministry of Finance), where the Alta Semita and Vicus Longus met; start of the Via Salaria and Via Nomentana. Vestals convicted of unchastity were buried alive just inside at the Campus Sceleratus. Facing set by hand (gate at a corner of the circuit).

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Porta Quirinalis
g:porta_quirinalis.note: Gate near the temple of Quirinus on the north edge of the Quirinal, near Via delle Quattro Fontane (Festus 303 L).

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Porta Salutaris
g:porta_salutaris.note: Gate named from the temple of Salus, at the head of Via della Dataria (the Clivus Salutis).

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Porta Sanqualis
Coarelli, Rome and Environs (2007) 15
g:porta_sanqualis.note: Gate named from the shrine of Semo Sancus, at Largo Magnanapoli (wall remains in the central bed). Lost in the Trajanic works on the Quirinal slope (end date assumed). Facing set by hand (gate at a corner of the circuit).

phases.t: Porticus from the gate to the Ara Martis in the Campus (Livy 35.10.12).

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Porta Fontinalis
Richardson, NTDAR (1992) 302
g:porta_fontinalis.note: On the saddle between the Arx and the Quirinal, in front of the Museo del Risorgimento: the Clivus Argentarius led up to it and the Via Lata / Flaminia began outside, past the tomb of Bibulus. In 193 BC a porticus was built from the gate to the altar of Mars (Livy 35.10.12). Destroyed with the saddle for Trajan's Forum (end date assumed). Perhaps the Porta Ratumena of the earlier wall. Facing set by hand (gate at a corner of the circuit).

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Porta Ratumena
Richardson, NTDAR (1992) 309
g:porta_ratumena.note: Gate of the Arx toward the Campus Martius, named from the Veientine charioteer Ratumenna (Plutarch, Poplicola 13; Pliny NH 8.161). Possibly the predecessor of the Porta Fontinalis. Facing set by hand (gate at a corner of the circuit).

scholarship: Richardson, NTDAR (1992) 302
g:porta_catularia.note: Known from Festus (39 L) as a gate near the Capitol where red dogs were sacrificed; placed at the foot of the Capitol near the Carmentalis. Site wholly uncertain.

phases.t: Built with the wall: single arch between two towers.
Honorian rebuilding (401-403): travertine facing and raised towers.
Witiges tries the gate; Belisarius holds it (Procopius 5.23.3).

scholarship: Richmond, The City Wall of Imperial Rome (1930)
Platner-Ashby, Porta Flaminia
g:porta_flaminia.note: Northern gate on the Via Flaminia at the foot of the Pincian, beside the river wall. Honorian gate with a single travertine arch between two semicircular towers; the present Porta del Popolo facade is of 1562-65 and its towers of Sixtus IV (1475). Faces north.

phases.t: Postern.
Honorian rebuilding (401-403): upgraded to a gate with two semicircular towers.
Belisarius holds the Pinciana and Salaria sector.

scholarship: Richmond, The City Wall of Imperial Rome (1930)
Platner-Ashby, Porta Pinciana
Cozza, BullCom 1987
g:porta_pinciana.note: Gate on the Via Salaria Vetus (Via Pinciana), originally a postern; given travertine facing and two semicircular towers by Honorius. Belisarius' command post during the siege (Procopius 5.19.14); the medieval legend of Belisarius begging here.

phases.t: Built over tombs of the Via Salaria.
Honorian rebuilding (401-403): raised, travertine facing.
24 August 410: Alaric enters here.
Main Gothic assault on the north side (Procopius 5.22.1).

scholarship: Richmond, The City Wall of Imperial Rome (1930)
Platner-Ashby, Porta Salaria
g:porta_salaria.note: Gate of the Via Salaria Nova, demolished in 1871 after damage in the 1870 assault and rebuilt by Vespignani (removed 1921). Single arch between semicircular towers; tombs (Q. Sulpicius Maximus) found in the towers.

phases.t: Built with the wall.
Honorian rebuilding (401-403): travertine facing and semicircular towers.

scholarship: Richmond, The City Wall of Imperial Rome (1930)
Platner-Ashby, Porta Nomentana
g:porta_nomentana.note: Gate of the Via Nomentana, 75 m east of Michelangelo's Porta Pia (1561-65), which replaced it; walled up by Pius IV in 1564. The right tower survives; the left was demolished in 1827. Single arch between semicircular towers (Honorian travertine).

scholarship: Richmond, The City Wall of Imperial Rome (1930)
g:postern_montebello.note: One of the posterns near the Porta Nomentana and the camp's NW corner closed under Honorius (it.wikipedia, Mura aureliane). Position approximate.

phases.t: Camp gate.
Blocked, open no longer.

scholarship: Richardson, NTDAR (1992) 78-79
g:castra_porta_principalis_sinistra.note: Gate of the praetorian camp in the north side, walled up when Aurelian absorbed the camp; the blocked arch is still visible. OSM labels it Porta Praetoriana.

phases.t: Camp gate.
Blocked.

scholarship: Richardson, NTDAR (1992) 78-79
g:castra_porta_principalis_dextra.note: East gate of the camp (Porta Principalis Dextera in OSM), blocked when the camp entered the Aurelian circuit.

phases.t: Built with the wall.
Possibly closed in the Honorian works.

scholarship: Richmond, The City Wall of Imperial Rome (1930)
Platner-Ashby, Vicus Collis Viminalis
g:porta_chiusa.note: Gate on Viale Pretoriano south of the camp, closed already in antiquity (name medieval); single arch flanked by a square tower. Probably the end of the Vicus Collis Viminalis road.

phases.t: Augustan aqueduct arch over the road.
Aqueduct arch becomes the gate.
Honorian rebuilding (401-403): outer gate court and facade, inscription naming Arcadius and Honorius, at the suggestion of Stilicho.

scholarship: Richmond, The City Wall of Imperial Rome (1930)
Platner-Ashby, Porta Tiburtina
g:porta_tiburtina.note: Gate of the Via Tiburtina built against the travertine arch that carried the Aquae Marcia, Tepula and Julia over the road (Augustus, 5 BC; restored by Titus and Caracalla). Honorius added an outer travertine gatehouse with a single arch and square towers and the dedication of 401-402 (CIL VI 1189). Porta S. Lorenzo in the Middle Ages.

phases.t: Claudian aqueduct crossing built.
Becomes a gate of the wall.
Honorian rebuilding (401-403): outer gate with towers over the Eurysaces tomb; inscription CIL VI 1188.
Witiges' main camp opposite; Gothic assault at the Vivarium just south (Procopius 5.22-23).

scholarship: Richmond, The City Wall of Imperial Rome (1930)
Coarelli, Rome and Environs (2007) 197-199
g:porta_praenestina_labicana.note: Double arch of the Aqua Claudia and Anio Novus over the forking Via Praenestina and Via Labicana (AD 52, travertine, rusticated, attic with the inscriptions of Claudius, Vespasian 71 and Titus 81), turned into a two-bay gate in 271. Honorius built an outer gatehouse with towers over the tomb of Eurysaces (demolished 1838). One of the two gates (with the Portuensis) to keep two bays. Height to the top of the attic about 24 m.

phases.t: Postern-type gate.
Honorian rebuilding (401-403): semicircular towers added.
Belisarius enters Rome (9-10 December).
Betrayed to Totila (Procopius 7.20.14-19).

scholarship: Richmond, The City Wall of Imperial Rome (1930)
Platner-Ashby, Porta Asinaria
g:porta_asinaria.note: Gate on the Via Asinaria next to the later Porta S. Giovanni (1574). Originally a postern with a single travertine arch; Honorius added two semicircular towers and a gatehouse. Through it Belisarius entered in 536 and Totila's Goths were let in by Isaurian guards on 17 December 546.

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Porta Metrovia
Richmond, The City Wall of Imperial Rome (1930)
g:porta_metrovia.note: Postern at the bend of the wall below the Caelian where the Marrana stream passed under the wall; mentioned by Gregory the Great (Epist. 9.69 'porta Metrovia'). Single small arch beside a square tower.

phases.t: Built with the wall.
Honorian rebuilding (401-403): travertine arch, towers raised.
Walled up during the siege? (uncertain).

scholarship: Richmond, The City Wall of Imperial Rome (1930)
Platner-Ashby, Porta Latina
g:porta_latina.note: Gate of the Via Latina with a single travertine arch (keystone with chi-rho on the outer face, Honorian or later) flanked by semicircular towers; the inner face is brick. Close to the church of S. Giovanni a Porta Latina.

phases.t: Double-arched gate, semicircular towers.
Honorian rebuild: single arch, attic, square tower bases.
Greek inscription to SS Conon and George (6th-7th century).

scholarship: Richmond, The City Wall of Imperial Rome (1930)
Museo delle Mura (Porta S. Sebastiano)
Platner-Ashby, Porta Appia
g:porta_appia.note: The grandest gate, on the Via Appia. Aurelian's gate had two arches and two semicircular towers with a travertine facade; Honorius (401-402) reduced it to one arch, added a high attic with two rows of six windows and an open crenellated walkway, set the towers on square marble-faced bases, and joined them to the 'Arch of Drusus' (the arch of the Aqua Antoniniana) behind by two walls forming a courtyard. A storey was added later. Towers here estimated at about 26 m.

scholarship: Richmond, The City Wall of Imperial Rome (1930)
Platner-Ashby, Porta Ardeatina
g:porta_ardeatina.note: Minor gate on the Via Ardeatina, between the Appia and the Ostiensis; obliterated by Antonio da Sangallo's bastion (1537-42). Simple arch without towers. Facing set by hand (gate at a corner of the circuit).

phases.t: Double outer arch.
Single outer arch, towers raised, inner double-arched court.
Opened to Totila by the Isaurians (Procopius 7.36.7).

scholarship: Richmond, The City Wall of Imperial Rome (1930)
Museo della Via Ostiense (Porta S. Paolo)
Platner-Ashby, Porta Ostiensis
g:porta_ostiensis.note: Gate of the Via Ostiensis beside the Pyramid of Cestius. Aurelian's outer facade had two arches between semicircular towers; Honorius reduced the outer face to one arch, raised the towers and added an inner court whose city face keeps two arches. Totila took Rome when Isaurian guards opened it (549/550).

scholarship: Richmond, The City Wall of Imperial Rome (1930)
g:postern_pyramid.note: Postern in the stretch between the Pyramid and the Tiber, closed by Maxentius and demolished in 1888 (it.wikipedia, Mura aureliane). Position approximate. Facing set by hand (gate at a corner of the circuit).

phases.t: Two-arched gate.
Honorian rebuilding (401-403): two arches retained, gate and towers raised.

scholarship: Richmond, The City Wall of Imperial Rome (1930)
Platner-Ashby, Porta Portuensis
g:porta_portuensis.note: Southern gate of the Trastevere salient at the start of the Via Portuensis and Via Campana, at the junction of Via Portuense and Via E. Bezzi, about 450 m south of Porta Portese (1644) which replaced it when Urban VIII demolished the Janiculum walls. Honorius kept two arches, raised gate and towers and set up an inscription like those of the Tiburtina and Praenestina (CIL VI 1190). Tower form assumed.

phases.t: Built with the wall.
Held by Paulus during the siege (Procopius 5.18.35, 5.23.12).

scholarship: Richmond, The City Wall of Imperial Rome (1930)
Platner-Ashby, Porta Aurelia
g:porta_aurelia.note: Gate on the Janiculum summit where the Via Aurelia Vetus left Trastevere, called Porta S. Pancratii from the 6th century (Procopius 5.18.35). Destroyed in the 1849 siege and rebuilt by Vespignani (1854). Tower form unknown. Facing set by hand (gate at a corner of the circuit).

scholarship: Richmond, The City Wall of Imperial Rome (1930)
Platner-Ashby, Porta Septimiana
g:porta_septimiana.note: Northern gate of the Trastevere salient at the start of Via della Lungara; the name may recall Septimius Severus (the Horti Getae nearby). Rebuilt in 1498 by Alexander VI with Ghibelline merlons.

scholarship: Richmond, The City Wall of Imperial Rome (1930)
Platner-Ashby, Porta Cornelia
g:porta_aurelia_sancti_petri.note: River-wall gate at the left-bank end of the Pons Aelius, through which the road to the Vatican and the Via Cornelia passed; Procopius' 'Aurelian gate, now named after Peter' (5.19.4). Covered after 403 by the fortified Mausoleum of Hadrian across the river. Form unknown.

scholarship: it.wikipedia, Mura aureliane
Richmond, The City Wall of Imperial Rome (1930)
g:postern_tor_di_nona.note: One of the small landing-stage posterns of the Campus Martius river wall; the medieval Torre dell'Annona (Tor di Nona) stood on the wall here. Some identify a 'Porta Domitia' near it.

scholarship: it.wikipedia, Mura aureliane
g:postern_ripetta.note: Posterula in the river wall opposite the Mausoleum of Augustus, where river traffic landed (later Porto di Ripetta). Illustrative position.

p:statio_cohors_i_vigilum.summary: Barracks of the cohort covering Regions VII (Via Lata) and IX (Circus Flaminius). Remains seen in the 17th century between San Marcello al Corso and Santi Apostoli included large halls and statues, among them a Genius of the cohort, and many dedications to emperors by the cohort come from the same spot.
scholarship: Sablayrolles, Libertinus miles: les cohortes de vigiles (1996)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
Lanciani, Forma Urbis Romae (1893-1901) pl. 22
p:statio_cohors_i_vigilum.note: End date conjectural: the vigiles are last securely attested in the 4th century; fire-fighting passed to the urban prefecture and the collegia. Position from the 1644 discoveries reported by Lanciani; the barracks probably filled a whole block west of Piazza Santi Apostoli.

p:statio_cohors_ii_vigilum.summary: Station of the cohort for Regions III and V, on the Esquiline plateau near the later church of Santa Bibiana, inside the Aurelian circuit and just behind the line of the Servian agger. Vigiles inscriptions found here and Pirro Ligorio's note of a large building destroyed in the 16th century fix the area.
scholarship: Sablayrolles, Libertinus miles: les cohortes de vigiles (1996)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
p:statio_cohors_ii_vigilum.note: End date conjectural: the vigiles are last securely attested in the 4th century; fire-fighting passed to the urban prefecture and the collegia. Exact footprint unknown; placed on Via Giolitti by Santa Bibiana.

p:statio_cohors_iii_vigilum.summary: Station of the cohort for Regions IV and VI, listed by the Regionary Catalogues in Region VI (Alta Semita). Vigiles inscriptions south of the Baths of Diocletian suggest it stood on the Viminal ridge between the baths and the Vicus Patricius.
scholarship: Sablayrolles, Libertinus miles: les cohortes de vigiles (1996)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
p:statio_cohors_iii_vigilum.note: End date conjectural: the vigiles are last securely attested in the 4th century; fire-fighting passed to the urban prefecture and the collegia. Only the general area is known.

p:statio_cohors_iv_vigilum.summary: Station of the cohort for Regions XII and XIII, on the Piccolo Aventino by the church of San Saba. Inscriptions naming the cohort, including dedications by its officers, were found around San Saba and fix the barracks there, controlling the Aventine and the Emporium below.
scholarship: Sablayrolles, Libertinus miles: les cohortes de vigiles (1996)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
p:statio_cohors_iv_vigilum.note: End date conjectural: the vigiles are last securely attested in the 4th century; fire-fighting passed to the urban prefecture and the collegia.

p:statio_cohors_v_vigilum.summary: Station of the cohort for Regions I and II, on the Caelian beside and below Santa Maria in Domnica (the Navicella). Two large marble rosters of the cohort dated AD 205 and 210 (CIL VI 1057-1058) and altars to the Genius of its centuries were found here in the 19th century, with a courtyard and portico.
scholarship: Sablayrolles, Libertinus miles: les cohortes de vigiles (1996)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
p:statio_cohors_v_vigilum.note: End date conjectural: the vigiles are last securely attested in the 4th century; fire-fighting passed to the urban prefecture and the collegia. The rosters list over 1,000 men, showing the cohort's strength after Septimius Severus.

p:statio_cohors_vi_vigilum.summary: Station of the cohort for Regions VIII and X, placed by the Regionary Catalogues in Region VIII near the imperial fora. Its site has not been found; it probably lay on the slope between the Forum of Caesar and the Capitol along the Clivus Argentarius.
scholarship: Sablayrolles, Libertinus miles: les cohortes de vigiles (1996)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
p:statio_cohors_vi_vigilum.note: End date conjectural: the vigiles are last securely attested in the 4th century; fire-fighting passed to the urban prefecture and the collegia. Location is a guess within Region VIII.

p:statio_cohors_vii_vigilum.summary: Main barracks of the cohort for Regions XI and XIV (Transtiberim). Unlike its excavated guardhouse by San Crisogono, the station itself is unlocated; it probably stood in the dense lowland of Trastevere between Santa Maria in Trastevere and the river crossing at the Pons Aemilius.
scholarship: Sablayrolles, Libertinus miles: les cohortes de vigiles (1996)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
p:statio_cohors_vii_vigilum.note: End date conjectural: the vigiles are last securely attested in the 4th century; fire-fighting passed to the urban prefecture and the collegia.

p:excubitorium_cohors_vii.summary: Guardhouse of the seventh cohort excavated in 1866-1867 about 20 m south of San Crisogono, at the corner of Via di Monte Fiore and Via della VII Coorte. A Hadrianic house with a hexagonal basin in its court and a shrine (lararium) was converted into a post; more than 100 graffiti of the vigiles, dated AD 215-245 and invoking the 'Genius excubitori', cover its walls. The upper part stands about 8 m above the ancient floor.
scholarship: Sablayrolles, Libertinus miles: les cohortes de vigiles (1996)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
Mols, 'L'excubitorium della VII coorte a Trastevere', Mededelingen Rome (2002)
p:excubitorium_cohors_vii.note: Reburied in 1966. Built as a house under Hadrian (brick stamps), used by the vigiles in the early 3rd century; the aedicula paintings are Severan.

p:excubitorium_regio_i.summary: One of the 14 guard posts listed by the 4th-century Regionary Catalogues ('cohortes VII vigilum habentes excubitoria XIIII'). Region I had no main station; its post, manned from the cohort V, probably stood beside the Via Appia south of the Porta Capena, between the Baths of Caracalla and the Caelian.
scholarship: Sablayrolles, Libertinus miles: les cohortes de vigiles (1996)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
p:excubitorium_regio_i.note: Follows the view that the 14 excubitoria include the 7 stations, leaving one post in each of the 7 regions without a station. Position is a reasoned guess on a main street of the region. End date conjectural: the vigiles are last securely attested in the 4th century; fire-fighting passed to the urban prefecture and the collegia.

p:excubitorium_regio_iii.summary: One of the 14 guard posts listed by the 4th-century Regionary Catalogues ('cohortes VII vigilum habentes excubitoria XIIII'). Region III had no main station; its post, manned from the cohort I, probably stood in the Oppian valley along the Via Labicana near the Ludus Magnus.
scholarship: Sablayrolles, Libertinus miles: les cohortes de vigiles (1996)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
p:excubitorium_regio_iii.note: Follows the view that the 14 excubitoria include the 7 stations, leaving one post in each of the 7 regions without a station. Position is a reasoned guess on a main street of the region. End date conjectural: the vigiles are last securely attested in the 4th century; fire-fighting passed to the urban prefecture and the collegia.

p:excubitorium_regio_iv.summary: One of the 14 guard posts listed by the 4th-century Regionary Catalogues ('cohortes VII vigilum habentes excubitoria XIIII'). Region IV had no main station; its post, manned from the cohort III, probably stood in the Subura near the Vicus Patricius and the Clivus Suburanus.
scholarship: Sablayrolles, Libertinus miles: les cohortes de vigiles (1996)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes

Position is a reasoned guess on a main street of the region. End date conjectural: the vigiles are last securely attested in the 4th century; fire-fighting passed to the urban prefecture and the collegia.

p:excubitorium_regio_ix.summary: One of the 14 guard posts listed by the 4th-century Regionary Catalogues ('cohortes VII vigilum habentes excubitoria XIIII'). Region IX had no main station; its post, manned from the cohort I, probably stood in the central Campus Martius between the Theatre of Pompey and the Pantheon.
scholarship: Sablayrolles, Libertinus miles: les cohortes de vigiles (1996)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes

Position is a reasoned guess on a main street of the region. End date conjectural: the vigiles are last securely attested in the 4th century; fire-fighting passed to the urban prefecture and the collegia.

p:excubitorium_regio_x.summary: One of the 14 guard posts listed by the 4th-century Regionary Catalogues ('cohortes VII vigilum habentes excubitoria XIIII'). Region X had no main station; its post, manned from the cohort VI, probably stood on the Clivus Victoriae at the north-west corner of the Palatine.
scholarship: Sablayrolles, Libertinus miles: les cohortes de vigiles (1996)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
p:excubitorium_regio_x.note: Follows the view that the 14 excubitoria include the 7 stations, leaving one post in each of the 7 regions without a station. Position is a reasoned guess on a main street of the region. End date conjectural: the vigiles are last securely attested in the 4th century; fire-fighting passed to the urban prefecture and the collegia.

p:excubitorium_regio_xi.summary: One of the 14 guard posts listed by the 4th-century Regionary Catalogues ('cohortes VII vigilum habentes excubitoria XIIII'). Region XI had no main station; its post, manned from the cohort VII, probably stood in the Forum Boarium and Velabrum by the starting gates of the Circus Maximus.
scholarship: Sablayrolles, Libertinus miles: les cohortes de vigiles (1996)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
p:excubitorium_regio_xi.note: Follows the view that the 14 excubitoria include the 7 stations, leaving one post in each of the 7 regions without a station. Position is a reasoned guess on a main street of the region. End date conjectural: the vigiles are last securely attested in the 4th century; fire-fighting passed to the urban prefecture and the collegia.

p:excubitorium_regio_xiii.summary: One of the 14 guard posts listed by the 4th-century Regionary Catalogues ('cohortes VII vigilum habentes excubitoria XIIII'). Region XIII had no main station; its post, manned from the cohort IV, probably stood on the river slope of the Aventine above the Emporium.
scholarship: Sablayrolles, Libertinus miles: les cohortes de vigiles (1996)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
