Position is a reasoned guess on a main street of the region. End date conjectural: the vigiles are last securely attested in the 4th century; fire-fighting passed to the urban prefecture and the collegia.

p:statio_praefecti_vigilum.summary: Office of the equestrian prefect commanding the 3,500 to 7,000 vigiles, with judicial powers over arson, burglary and theft. Its site is unknown; scholars have suggested the area of the Crypta Balbi or the station of the first cohort by Santi Apostoli.
scholarship: Sablayrolles, Libertinus miles: les cohortes de vigiles (1996)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
p:statio_praefecti_vigilum.note: Placed at the Crypta Balbi hypothesis; the alternative is the First Cohort's station.

p:castra_praetoria_institution.summary: Sejanus concentrated the nine (later more) praetorian cohorts, until then billeted around Rome and Italy, in a single camp on the Viminal plateau in AD 23; the urban cohorts shared it. It became the arena of imperial politics: Claudius was proclaimed here in 41, the empire auctioned here in 193. Constantine abolished the guard after the Milvian Bridge in 312 and demolished the inner wall.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Castra Praetoria
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000) s.v. Castra Praetoria
p:castra_praetoria_institution.note: The physical camp is in the buildings collection (castra_praetoria_mon); this record carries the institution.

p:castra_urbana.summary: The urban cohorts, the city police under the praefectus urbi, lived in the Castra Praetoria until Aurelian gave them their own camp 'in campo Agrippae' in the 270s. It lay in Region VII east of the Via Lata, near the Forum Suarium whose pork distribution the cohorts supervised.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Castra Urbana
Coarelli, Rome and Environs: An Archaeological Guide (2007)
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000) s.v. Castra Urbana
p:castra_urbana.note: Exact site unknown; placed in the Campus Agrippae between Via del Corso and Via del Tritone.

p:castra_peregrina.summary: Camp on the Caelian of the frumentarii and other soldiers seconded from the provincial armies, who acted as couriers, supply officers and secret police. Remains, dedications to the Genius castrorum peregrinorum and a mithraeum were found under and north of Santo Stefano Rotondo.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Castra Peregrina
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000) s.v. Castra Peregrina

p:castra_priora_equitum_singularium.summary: First barracks of the emperor's horse guard, the equites singulares Augusti, founded under Trajan. Remains with many altars of the guardsmen came to light in 1885-1886 on Via Tasso, north of the Lateran.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Castra Equitum Singularium
Speidel, Riding for Caesar (1994)
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000)
p:castra_priora_equitum_singularium.note: Disbanded by Constantine in 312 for supporting Maxentius.

p:castra_nova_equitum_singularium.summary: Second barracks of the imperial horse guard, built under Septimius Severus when he doubled the unit. Constantine razed it after 312 and built the Lateran basilica on top; its walls and painted rooms survive beneath the nave of San Giovanni in Laterano.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)
Speidel, Riding for Caesar (1994)

p:castra_misenatium.summary: Quarters of the detachment of sailors from the fleet at Misenum, who worked the great awnings (velaria) of the Colosseum and staged naval shows. The Regionary Catalogues place it in Region III, near the amphitheatre along the Via Labicana.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Castra Misenatium
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000)
p:castra_misenatium.note: Exact site uncertain; placed east of the Ludus Magnus.

p:castra_ravennatium.summary: Quarters in Trastevere of the sailors of the Ravenna fleet, probably connected with the naumachiae on the right bank. Listed in Region XIV by the Regionary Catalogues; often placed near San Callisto.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Castra Ravennatium
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000)

p:castra_lecticariorum.summary: Barracks of the litter-bearers' guild in Region XIV, listed in the Regionary Catalogues. The litter carriers of the wealthy were organised as a corporation and lodged together in Trastevere.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Castra Lecticariorum
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000)

p:statio_urbana_templum_pacis.summary: The hall on the south-east side of Vespasian's Templum Pacis, whose wall carried the Severan Marble Plan (203-211), is widely taken to have housed the records of the urban prefecture and the city survey. The plan's 150 marble slabs, 18 by 13 m, show every building at 1:240.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)
Tucci, The Temple of Peace in Rome (2017)
Stanford Digital Forma Urbis Romae Project
p:statio_urbana_templum_pacis.note: The hall survives as the rear wall of Santi Cosma e Damiano (527). Function as prefecture office is inferred.

p:secretarium_tellurense.summary: In late antiquity the urban prefect heard cases at the secretarium by the Temple of Tellus on the Carinae; the acts of the martyrs and the Theodosian Code place trials 'in Tellure'. The temple had been built in 268 BC on the site of Spurius Cassius' razed house.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Tellus, Aedes
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000) s.v. Secretarium Tellurense
Krautheimer, Rome: Profile of a City, 312-1308 (1980)
p:secretarium_tellurense.note: Near San Pietro in Vincoli and Via del Colosseo.

p:statio_annonae.summary: Late 4th-century arcaded hall of the grain office by the Forum Boarium, whose columns are still embedded in the walls of Santa Maria in Cosmedin. It administered the annona, the free and subsidised food supply of the city; by the late 6th century it had become a diaconia distributing church relief.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Statio Annonae
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)
Krautheimer, Rome: Profile of a City, 312-1308 (1980)
p:statio_annonae.note: Earlier offices of the praefectus annonae stood nearby around the Ara Maxima.

p:statio_aquarum.summary: Office of the curator aquarum, moved in the early 4th century to rooms beside the spring of Juturna in the Forum. Inscriptions of the curators of 328 and later were found in the rooms; the water board controlled the aqueducts until their cutting by the Goths in 537.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Statio Aquarum
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000)

p:mensa_ponderaria_castoris.summary: The Temple of Castor in the Forum served as the bureau of weights and measures: official bronze and stone weights are inscribed as checked 'ad Castoris', and the podium chambers held deposits and bankers' strongboxes. Here traders had scales and measures tested against the public standards.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Castor, Aedes
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929)
Nielsen and Poulsen, The Temple of Castor and Pollux I (1992)
p:mensa_ponderaria_castoris.note: Mensa ponderaria is the generic term for a standard-measure table; the Roman one sat at this temple.

p:lautumiae.summary: Old quarry-prison on the north-west side of the Forum, below the Arx, next to the Carcer. Livy names it in the fire of 210 BC with the Forum Piscarium, and Carthaginian hostages were kept here; the area was cleared for the Forum of Caesar.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Lautumiae
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929)

p:curia_hostilia_senate.summary: The traditional Senate house at the north side of the Comitium, facing south. The Senate met here through the Republic; it was burned by Clodius' supporters who cremated his body inside in January 52 BC, rebuilt by Faustus Sulla and cleared by Caesar for the Curia Iulia.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Bonnefond-Coudry, Le Sénat de la République romaine (1989)

p:curia_iulia_senate.summary: Caesar's new Senate house, dedicated by Augustus in 29 BC and rebuilt by Diocletian after the fire of 283. The last recorded act of the Senate is the reception of Phocas' images in 603; Honorius I turned the hall into the church of Sant'Adriano in 630.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Bonnefond-Coudry, Le Sénat de la République romaine (1989)

p:curia_pompeia_senate.summary: Hall at the east end of Pompey's portico, used by the Senate while the Curia Hostilia lay in ruins. Caesar was murdered here at the foot of Pompey's statue on 15 March 44 BC; Augustus walled it up as an accursed place.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Bonnefond-Coudry, Le Sénat de la République romaine (1989)

p:temple_concord_senate.summary: A frequent meeting place of the Senate: Cicero's fourth Catilinarian (63 BC) and the condemnation of Sejanus (AD 31) were delivered here.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Bonnefond-Coudry, Le Sénat de la République romaine (1989)

p:temple_jupiter_senate.summary: The new consuls convened the Senate in the Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus on the first day of their year, after their sacrifice.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Bonnefond-Coudry, Le Sénat de la République romaine (1989)

p:temple_bellona_senate.summary: Because it stood outside the pomerium, the Senate met here to receive generals still holding imperium and foreign embassies not admitted to the city. Sulla had 6,000 prisoners massacred in the Villa Publica within earshot of a meeting here in 82 BC.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Bonnefond-Coudry, Le Sénat de la République romaine (1989)

p:temple_apollo_medicus_senate.summary: Next to the Temple of Bellona in the Prata Flaminia, also used for Senate meetings outside the pomerium, especially to debate triumphs.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Bonnefond-Coudry, Le Sénat de la République romaine (1989)

p:temple_jupiter_stator_senate.summary: Here, on 8 November 63 BC, Cicero delivered the First Catilinarian to a Senate guarded by armed men, with Catiline present.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Bonnefond-Coudry, Le Sénat de la République romaine (1989)

p:temple_fides_senate.summary: On the Capitol near the Temple of Jupiter. The Senate was meeting here in 133 BC when Scipio Nasica led the senators out to kill Tiberius Gracchus.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Bonnefond-Coudry, Le Sénat de la République romaine (1989)

p:temple_tellus_senate.summary: On the Carinae near Antony's house. Two days after Caesar's murder the Senate met here and, on Cicero's motion, voted an amnesty for the assassins while confirming Caesar's acts.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Bonnefond-Coudry, Le Sénat de la République romaine (1989)

p:temple_castor_senate.summary: The Senate occasionally met in the temple, whose high podium also served as a speakers' platform for assemblies in the Forum.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Bonnefond-Coudry, Le Sénat de la République romaine (1989)

p:library_apollo_senate.summary: In his old age Augustus often held Senate meetings in the Latin library hall of the Palatine Temple of Apollo, and revised the senatorial lists there.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Bonnefond-Coudry, Le Sénat de la République romaine (1989)

p:temple_mars_ultor_senate.summary: Augustus decreed that the Senate should deliberate here on wars and triumphs, and that victorious generals should dedicate their sceptres and crowns to Mars.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Bonnefond-Coudry, Le Sénat de la République romaine (1989)

p:senaculum.summary: Open waiting place of the senators between the Comitium and the Temple of Concord, where they assembled before meetings in the Curia.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Bonnefond-Coudry, Le Sénat de la République romaine (1989)

p:secretarium_senatus.summary: Late-antique court room behind the Curia, where the Senate tried senators. It was restored by the urban prefect Epiphanius in 412 after the Gothic sack; the church of Santa Martina later occupied it.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Bonnefond-Coudry, Le Sénat de la République romaine (1989)

p:macellum_republican.summary: The general provisions market behind the Basilica Aemilia, built by the censor M. Fulvius Nobilior in 179 BC by surrounding the older fish and delicacy markets with shops. Varro describes it as the union of the specialised fora. It burned in 64 and Vespasian's Templum Pacis was built over its site.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Macellum
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929)
De Ruyt, Macellum (1983)
p:macellum_republican.note: Position under the north-west part of the Templum Pacis, reached from the Argiletum.

p:forum_piscarium.summary: The fish market north of the Forum, where Plautus' characters bargain for fish. It burned with the Lautumiae and the Atrium Regium in the arson of 210 BC and was rebuilt, then absorbed in 179 BC into Fulvius' Macellum.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Forum Piscarium
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929)

p:forum_cuppedinis.summary: Market for luxury foods and dainties (cuppedia) near the Sacra Via, north-east of the Forum. Varro derives its name from the dainties or from a knight Cuppes whose house stood there; it became part of the Macellum complex.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Forum Cuppedinis
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929)

p:macellum_liviae.summary: Provisions market on the Esquiline just outside the Porta Esquilina, dedicated by Tiberius in 7 BC in Livia's name. It served the new Esquiline quarter; Valentinian, Valens and Gratian restored it in 364-367.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Macellum Liviae
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929)
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000)
De Ruyt, Macellum (1983)
p:macellum_liviae.note: Placed between the Arch of Gallienus and Santa Maria Maggiore's eastern slope, near San Vito; site not excavated.

p:macellum_magnum.summary: Great market on the Caelian dedicated by Nero in 59 and shown on his coins as a two-storey building with a domed central pavilion. Santo Stefano Rotondo (c. 470) is commonly thought to stand on its site and perhaps to echo its round plan.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Macellum Magnum
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929)
De Ruyt, Macellum (1983)
p:macellum_magnum.note: Identification with the site of Santo Stefano Rotondo is debated.

p:forum_esquilinum.summary: Market square just inside the Porta Esquilina. In 88 BC Sulla's troops entering the city fought Marius' supporters here; it later appears among the sights of Region V.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Forum Esquilinum
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929)

p:forum_suarium.summary: Pork market in the Campus Agrippae, Region VII, under a tribunus fori suarii and the guild of the suarii. Aurelian added free pork to the dole in the 270s and the distribution was run from here; Valentinian III still regulated it in 452.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Forum Suarium
Barnish, 'Pigs, plebeians and potentes', PBSR 55 (1987)
p:forum_suarium.note: Site not found; placed by the Castra Urbana whose soldiers supervised it.

p:forum_vinarium.summary: Wholesale wine market known from inscriptions of merchants 'a foro vinario'. It lay near the river where wine arrived by barge, probably by the Emporium below the Aventine or across the river at Ripa.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Forum Vinarium
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929)
p:forum_vinarium.note: Location unknown; placed at the north end of the Emporium quays.

p:ciconiae_nixae.summary: Landing place in the north-west Campus Martius, named after a monument of 'leaning storks', where wine shipments were taxed. Aurelian's subsidised wine was stored in the porticoes of the Temple of Sol and distributed through this office.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Ciconiae Nixae
Coarelli, Rome and Environs: An Archaeological Guide (2007)
p:ciconiae_nixae.note: Coarelli places it near San Salvatore in Lauro.

p:forum_pistorum.summary: Bakers' market listed in Region XIII (Aventinus), presumably near the mills and grain warehouses of the Emporium.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Forum Pistorum
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929)

p:forum_boarium_market.summary: The cattle market by the river harbour, the oldest trading place of the city, where the Etruscan and Greek traders met the Latins at the ford below the Tiber Island. It stayed a market square through antiquity.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Forum Boarium
Coarelli, Rome and Environs: An Archaeological Guide (2007)

p:forum_holitorium_market.summary: Vegetable and herb market outside the Porta Carmentalis, between the Capitol and the river, with the temples of Janus, Spes and Juno Sospita along its west side.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Forum Holitorium
Coarelli, Rome and Environs: An Archaeological Guide (2007)

p:porticus_minucia_frumentaria.summary: The distribution centre of the frumentationes, the free monthly grain ration (5 modii) for some 200,000 registered citizens. Recipients carried tesserae naming a day and one of 45 numbered doors (ostia) of the portico. Aurelian replaced grain with daily bread handed out from steps (gradus) across the city.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Porticus Minucia
Coarelli, Rome and Environs: An Archaeological Guide (2007)
Virlouvet, Tessera frumentaria (1995)
p:porticus_minucia_frumentaria.note: Coarelli identifies the Frumentaria with the large portico east of Largo Argentina along Via delle Botteghe Oscure; Manacorda prefers the Crypta Balbi area. Distribution there probably began under Claudius.

p:bakery_eurysaces.summary: The freedman baker and contractor for public bread built his tomb (c. 30 BC) at the fork of the Via Praenestina and Labicana, its frieze showing grain weighed, milled by donkeys, kneaded, baked and delivered to officials. His bakery probably stood nearby at the city edge.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Sepulcrum Eurysacis
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)
Petersen, The Freedman in Roman Art and Art History (2006)
p:bakery_eurysaces.note: Bakery site inferred from the tomb; the tomb itself is in buildings (tomb_of_eurysaces). Regionary Catalogues count 254 bakeries (pistrina) in the city.

p:molae_ianiculi.summary: Water-mills driven by the Aqua Traiana on the Janiculum slope, partly excavated under the American Academy and along Via Garibaldi. In 537 the Goths cut the aqueducts and Belisarius kept the city fed by mounting mills on boats moored in the Tiber.
scholarship: Wilson, 'Water-mills on the Janiculum', MAAR 45 (2000)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)

p:floating_mills_537.summary: When the Goths cut the aqueducts in 537, Belisarius moored boats below the bridge at the Janiculum and hung mill-wheels between them in the current; the Goths sent logs and corpses downstream to break them, and he answered with chains across the river.
scholarship: Wilson, 'Water-mills on the Janiculum', MAAR 45 (2000)
Krautheimer, Rome: Profile of a City, 312-1308 (1980)
p:floating_mills_537.note: Near the Pons Aurelius (Ponte Sisto). Ship-mills remained typical of medieval Rome.

p:mill_baths_caracalla.summary: A water-mill driven by the outflow of the baths was installed in the underground service galleries of the Baths of Caracalla, one of the few urban mills known in Rome.
scholarship: Schiøler and Wikander, 'A Roman water-mill in the Baths of Caracalla', Opuscula Romana 14 (1983)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)

p:horrea_agrippiana.summary: Warehouse of three storeys around a courtyard at the foot of the Palatine on the Vicus Tuscus, built by Agrippa and rebuilt under Domitian. A shrine in the court held a statue base to the Genius horreorum Agrippianorum. Excavated in 1902-1904 by Boni beside San Teodoro.
scholarship: Rickman, Roman Granaries and Store Buildings (1971)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Horrea Agrippiana
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)
Astolfi, Guidobaldi and Pronti, 'Horrea Agrippiana', ArchCl 30 (1978)

p:horrea_germaniciana.summary: Listed with the Horrea Agrippiana in Region VIII; presumably named after Germanicus and standing beside them along the Vicus Tuscus towards the Velabrum.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Horrea Germaniciana
Rickman, Roman Granaries and Store Buildings (1971)

p:horrea_piperataria.summary: Spice warehouses built by Domitian on the Sacra Via for pepper and eastern spices. Their burning in the fire of 192 destroyed the stock of many merchants and the books Galen kept there. Maxentius levelled them for his Basilica Nova; their rooms lie under it.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Horrea Piperataria
Rickman, Roman Granaries and Store Buildings (1971)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)

p:horrea_vespasiani.summary: Warehouses attributed to Vespasian in the Chronographer of 354, probably near the Sacra Via close to the Horrea Piperataria, serving the luxury trade of the Velia.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Horrea Vespasiani
Rickman, Roman Granaries and Store Buildings (1971)

p:horrea_galbana.summary: The largest warehouse complex of Rome, about 167 by 146 m around three long courtyards behind the Emporium, with some 140 rooms per floor for grain, oil and wine. Built around 100 BC on land of the Sulpicii Galbae, perhaps by Ser. Sulpicius Galba (cos. 108 BC), and enlarged under the emperor Galba. Shown on the Marble Plan.
scholarship: Rickman, Roman Granaries and Store Buildings (1971)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Horrea Galbana
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)
Stanford Digital Forma Urbis Romae Project

p:horrea_lolliana.summary: Warehouse with two courtyards on the Tiber quay of the Emporium, named on fragment 25 of the Marble Plan, between the Porticus Aemilia and the river.
scholarship: Rickman, Roman Granaries and Store Buildings (1971)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Horrea Lolliana
Stanford Digital Forma Urbis Romae Project
p:horrea_lolliana.note: Builder perhaps a Lollius of the Augustan period.

p:horrea_seiana.summary: Warehouse known from inscriptions to the Genius of the horrea Seiana found near Testaccio; it probably stood south of the Horrea Galbana, perhaps named after Seius Strabo, father of Sejanus.
scholarship: Rickman, Roman Granaries and Store Buildings (1971)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Horrea Seiana

p:horrea_aniciana.summary: Warehouse named after the Anicii (or Anicetus), known from inscriptions found in the Testaccio district.
scholarship: Rickman, Roman Granaries and Store Buildings (1971)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)

p:horrea_candelaria.summary: Store for candles and tallow, shown on fragment 44 of the Marble Plan as a building around a large open area. Its location in the city has not been fixed.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Horrea Candelaria
Stanford Digital Forma Urbis Romae Project (fragment 44)
p:horrea_candelaria.note: Placed provisionally in the Velabrum; the true position is unknown.

p:horrea_chartaria.summary: Warehouse for papyrus and writing material listed in Region IV (Templum Pacis), conveniently near the booksellers of the Argiletum and the Vicus Sandaliarius.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Horrea Chartaria
Rickman, Roman Granaries and Store Buildings (1971)
p:horrea_chartaria.note: Exact site unknown within Region IV.

p:horrea_tinei_sacerdotis.summary: Private warehouse of the senator Q. Tineius Sacerdos (cos. 158 or his homonymous son, cos. 192), known from an inscription; likely in the Emporium district.
scholarship: Rickman, Roman Granaries and Store Buildings (1971)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)

p:horrea_ummidiana.summary: Warehouse named after the Ummidii, a senatorial family, known from inscriptions and the Marble Plan tradition; probably on the Aventine side of the city.
scholarship: Rickman, Roman Granaries and Store Buildings (1971)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
p:horrea_ummidiana.note: Location unknown; placed on the lower Aventine towards the Porta Raudusculana.

p:horrea_sempronia.summary: Public granaries built under Gaius Gracchus' grain law of 123 BC to store the grain sold at a fixed low price to citizens. Their site is unknown; most scholars look to the river below the Aventine.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Horrea Sempronia
Rickman, Roman Granaries and Store Buildings (1971)

p:horrea_volusiana.summary: Warehouse of the Volusii Saturnini, a great senatorial family of the early empire with a household of many hundreds of slaves, known from inscriptions; probably on the right bank near the Via Portuensis landing.
scholarship: Rickman, Roman Granaries and Store Buildings (1971)

p:horrea_via_lata.summary: A large arcaded building of the late empire on the Via Lata, interpreted as a public warehouse or porticus; its ground floor later housed the diaconia of Santa Maria in Via Lata.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Krautheimer, Rome: Profile of a City, 312-1308 (1980)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)
p:horrea_via_lata.note: Possibly part of the Saepta or the Porticus of the Via Lata complex.

p:latrina_via_garibaldi.summary: Public latrine on the Janiculum found in 1963 under the terrace in front of San Pietro in Montorio. A channel 0.4 m wide ran round three sides; the seats were probably wooden boards on supports. Frescoes and a geometric mosaic date it to the late 2nd or early 3rd century.
scholarship: Turismo Roma, Latrina romana di via Garibaldi
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)
p:latrina_via_garibaldi.note: Turismo Roma gives 41.8934 N, which falls on lower Via Garibaldi; placed here by the church terrace described in the excavation reports.

p:latrina_forum_caesaris.summary: Public latrine installed in the Trajanic rebuilding of the Forum of Caesar, in a room at its western corner by the Basilica Argentaria and the Clivus Argentarius, with marble seats along the walls over a flushing channel.
scholarship: Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)

p:latrina_largo_argentina.summary: Public latrine of the imperial period behind Temples A and B at Largo Argentina, beside the remains of the Curia of Pompey, serving the crowds of the Porticus Minucia and the theatres.
scholarship: Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)
Coarelli, Rome and Environs: An Archaeological Guide (2007)
p:latrina_largo_argentina.note: The Regionary Catalogues count 144 public latrines (foricae) in the city.

p:lacus_orphei.summary: Public fountain on the Esquiline at the top of the Clivus Suburanus, decorated with a figure of Orpheus surrounded by enchanted beasts and birds. Martial tells his book to climb past it to reach Pliny the Younger's house.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Lacus Orphei
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929)
p:lacus_orphei.note: Near Santa Lucia in Selci and San Martino ai Monti.

p:lacus_promethei.summary: Fountain with a statue group of Prometheus, listed in Region I (Porta Capena), probably on the Via Appia between the Porta Capena and the Baths of Caracalla.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Lacus Promethei
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929)

p:lacus_pastoris.summary: Fountain 'of the Shepherd' listed in Region III (Isis et Serapis), in the valley east of the Colosseum near the gladiatorial schools.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Lacus Pastoris
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929)

p:lacus_fundani.summary: Fountain on the lower Quirinal, possibly named after a Fundanius; it gave its name to the area where, in 63 BC, Catilinarian conspirators were said to have met.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Lacus Fundani
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929)
p:lacus_fundani.note: Tacitus places Flavian fighting near it in AD 69.

p:lacus_servilius.summary: Fountain basin at the west corner of the Basilica Iulia where the Vicus Iugarius entered the Forum. Sulla displayed the heads of the proscribed senators here in 82 BC; Agrippa adorned it with a hydra statue.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Lacus Servilius
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929)

p:lacus_ganymedis.summary: Fountain with a statue of Ganymede listed in the Regionary Catalogues, probably in the Campus Agrippae along the Via Lata.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Lacus Ganymedis

p:fons_camenarum.summary: Sacred spring in the grove of the Camenae and Egeria outside the Porta Capena, from which the Vestals drew the water for their rites. By Juvenal's day the grove was let to poor Jewish families.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Camenae
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929)
p:fons_camenarum.note: In the valley between the Caelian and the Aventine, by the Via Appia.

p:fons_mercurii.summary: Spring near the Porta Capena where merchants on the Ides of May sprinkled their goods and heads with laurel dipped in its water, asking Mercury to forgive their lies.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Fons Mercurii

p:agrippa_fountains_33bc.summary: As aedile in 33 BC Agrippa built 700 basins (lacus), 105 fountains and 130 distribution towers, many decorated with columns and statues. This marker stands for the network in the Campus Martius fed by his Aqua Virgo (19 BC).
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Evans, Water Distribution in Ancient Rome (1994)
p:agrippa_fountains_33bc.note: Symbolic marker; the 4th-century Regionary Catalogues count 1,352 lacus in the city.

p:compitum_acilium.summary: Crossroads shrine on the Velia. In 219 BC the state bought a shop here for Archagathus, the first Greek doctor in Rome. Its Augustan marble aedicula, dedicated by the vicomagistri in 5 BC, was found in 1932 when Via dell'Impero cut through the Velia.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Compitum Acilium
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000)
Lott, The Neighborhoods of Augustan Rome (2004)
p:compitum_acilium.note: Destroyed in the fire of 64 or the Neronian rebuilding; remains removed.

p:ara_vici_sandaliarii.summary: Marble compital altar of 2 BC (now in the Uffizi) from the Vicus Sandaliarius, the street of sandal-makers and booksellers in Region IV. Its reliefs show Augustus taking the augural staff with Gaius Caesar and Livia, the official image of the new Lares Augusti cult.
scholarship: Lott, The Neighborhoods of Augustan Rome (2004)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Vicus Sandaliarius
p:ara_vici_sandaliarii.note: Provenance within the street not recorded; placed near the Temple of Tellus.

p:ara_vici_aesculeti.summary: Compital altar dedicated in AD 2 by four magistri of the Vicus Aesculeti, found in situ in 1888 at the crossroads under Via Arenula in the southern Campus Martius. Its relief shows the vicomagistri sacrificing a pig and a bull.
scholarship: Lott, The Neighborhoods of Augustan Rome (2004)
Haselberger et al., Mapping Augustan Rome (2002)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Vicus Aesculeti
p:ara_vici_aesculeti.note: Now in the Capitoline collections (Centrale Montemartini).

p:sacellum_larum.summary: Shrine of the guardian Lares of the city at the top of the Sacra Via, at the north-east corner of the Palatine. It marked a corner of the Palatine pomerium of Romulus.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Lares, Sacellum
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929)

p:signum_vortumni.summary: Bronze statue of the Etruscan god Vertumnus in a small shrine where the Vicus Tuscus left the Forum behind the Temple of Castor. Propertius gives the statue a speaking voice; booksellers like the Sosii had stalls beside it.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Vortumnus, Signum
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929)
p:signum_vortumni.note: A base re-inscribed under Diocletian was found near the spot.

p:tigillum_sororium.summary: Wooden beam across a lane on the slope of the Carinae, under which the surviving Horatius was said to have passed to purify himself after killing his sister. The beam was renewed at public expense through antiquity.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Tigillum Sororium
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929)

p:ara_aius_locutius.summary: Altar to the 'Speaking Voice' at the foot of the Palatine near the Temple of Vesta, built where a plebeian heard a voice in the night warning of the coming Gauls in 391 BC, a warning the magistrates ignored.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Aius Locutius
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929)

p:puteal_libonis.summary: A fenced well-head in the Forum near the Arch of Fabius, struck by lightning and enclosed by a Scribonius Libo. Moneylenders, debtors and the praetor's tribunal gathered here, so Horace uses it as shorthand for the world of business.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Puteal Libonis
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929)

p:ianus_medius.summary: The middle of the arched passages beside the Basilica Aemilia, the meeting point of bankers and financiers. Horace and Cicero use 'the Ianus medius' as Romans now use 'Wall Street'.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Ianus Medius
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929)

p:library_atrium_libertatis.summary: The first public library of Rome, founded by Asinius Pollio from the spoils of his Illyrian campaign in the restored Atrium Libertatis, with Greek and Latin sections and portraits of authors, including the living Varro.
scholarship: Houston, Inside Roman Libraries (2014)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Atrium Libertatis
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000)
p:library_atrium_libertatis.note: The Atrium Libertatis is placed on the saddle between Capitol and Quirinal later cut for Trajan's Forum, where its functions passed to the Basilica Ulpia.

p:library_porticus_octaviae.summary: Greek and Latin libraries founded by Octavia in memory of her son Marcellus (d. 23 BC) inside her portico, managed by the grammarian C. Melissus. They burned in the fire of 80 and were restored.
scholarship: Houston, Inside Roman Libraries (2014)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Porticus Octaviae

p:library_apollo_palatinus.summary: Twin halls for Greek and Latin books beside Augustus' Temple of Apollo, with niches for book cupboards and portrait medallions of authors. Ovid's exiled books were barred from it. The temple burned in 363 and the library with it.
scholarship: Houston, Inside Roman Libraries (2014)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Bibliotheca Apollinis Palatini

p:library_templi_divi_augusti.summary: Library attached to the temple of the deified Augustus behind the Basilica Iulia, with a colossal bronze Apollo 50 feet high.
scholarship: Houston, Inside Roman Libraries (2014)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Augustus, Divus, Templum
p:library_templi_divi_augusti.note: The temple's site is unlocated; placed below the Palatine's north-west corner.

p:library_domus_tiberianae.summary: Imperial library in the palace on the Palatine above the Forum where Gellius and his friends sat reading and arguing over Latin usage.
scholarship: Houston, Inside Roman Libraries (2014)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)

p:library_templum_pacis.summary: Library in Vespasian's Temple of Peace, a meeting place of scholars and doctors. Galen lost books he had stored there and in the nearby warehouses in the fire of 192; Severus restored the complex.
scholarship: Houston, Inside Roman Libraries (2014)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Pax, Templum
Tucci, The Temple of Peace in Rome (2017)

p:library_ulpia.summary: The two library halls flanking Trajan's Column, one Greek and one Latin, with niches for book cupboards, which also held state archives such as praetors' edicts. Sidonius in the 450s and Venantius Fortunatus a century later still speak of readings and statues there.
scholarship: Houston, Inside Roman Libraries (2014)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Bibliotheca Ulpia

p:library_pantheon_africanus.summary: Julius Africanus, the Christian chronographer, designed 'the beautiful library in the Pantheon' for Severus Alexander, according to a papyrus fragment of his Kestoi. It was probably in the Baths of Agrippa or the Baths of Alexander next door.
scholarship: Houston, Inside Roman Libraries (2014)
p:library_pantheon_africanus.note: Exact position near the Pantheon uncertain.

p:library_baths_caracalla.summary: Two halls in the enclosure of the Baths of Caracalla, on either side of the stadium-shaped garden, with wall niches for book cupboards; baths combined bathing, exercise, lecture rooms and reading.
scholarship: Houston, Inside Roman Libraries (2014)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)
DeLaine, The Baths of Caracalla (1997)

p:library_baths_trajan.summary: Exedra on the south-west side of the enclosure of the Baths of Trajan fitted with tiered niches for books, among the clearest library rooms in Rome.
scholarship: Houston, Inside Roman Libraries (2014)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)

p:library_baths_diocletian.summary: The Historia Augusta claims that the books of the Bibliotheca Ulpia were in its day kept in the Baths of Diocletian, suggesting a library hall there.
scholarship: Houston, Inside Roman Libraries (2014)

p:library_capitolina.summary: Late sources record a library on the Capitol destroyed by lightning and fire under Commodus.
scholarship: Houston, Inside Roman Libraries (2014)

p:library_lucullus.summary: Lucullus opened his library of books captured in the Mithridatic War to Greek scholars in his gardens on the Pincian, with walks and study rooms; Cicero and Cato read there.
scholarship: Houston, Inside Roman Libraries (2014)
p:library_lucullus.note: In the Horti Lucullani; the gardens themselves are in buildings.

p:library_agapetus.summary: Pope Agapetus and Cassiodorus planned a Christian school at Rome around 535; Agapetus built a library on the Clivus Scauri, recorded in a verse inscription. A hall beside the monastery of Sant'Andrea has been identified with it.
scholarship: Krautheimer, Rome: Profile of a City, 312-1308 (1980)
Marrou, 'Autour de la bibliothèque du pape Agapit', MEFR 48 (1931)

p:archive_damasus.summary: Pope Damasus built a church and new buildings for the archives (archivis nova tecta) of the Roman church by the Theatre of Pompey, as his own verse inscription states; the site is now covered by the Palazzo della Cancelleria.
scholarship: Krautheimer, Rome: Profile of a City, 312-1308 (1980)
Pietri, Roma Christiana (1976)

p:scrinium_lateranense.summary: Archive and library of the bishop of Rome in the Lateran episcopium. Gregory the Great's registers of letters were kept here, and 7th-century popes sent books from it to England and Gaul.
scholarship: Krautheimer, Rome: Profile of a City, 312-1308 (1980)

p:athenaeum_hadriani.summary: Hadrian's institute for rhetoric, poetry and philosophy, where orators and poets declaimed. Three large halls with tiered marble seating for about 900 people were found in 2008-2012 under Piazza Venezia during work on Metro C.
scholarship: Egidi, Serlorenzi and others, excavation reports for Metro C at Piazza Venezia (2012)
p:athenaeum_hadriani.note: Identification with the Athenaeum is the excavators' and widely accepted.

p:school_plotinus.summary: From 244 until his last illness Plotinus taught Neoplatonism in Rome in the house of the widow Gemina, where senators like Rogatianus, the physician Eustochius and Porphyry heard him; the emperor Gallienus favoured him.
scholarship: Armstrong, Plotinus (Loeb) introduction
p:school_plotinus.note: The site of Gemina's house is unknown; placed on the Esquiline by convention only.

p:schola_xanthi.summary: Meeting hall of the scribes and heralds of the curule aediles at the foot of the Clivus Capitolinus beside the Temple of Saturn, restored by the freedman Bebryx Drusianus and Aulus Fabius Xanthus.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Schola Xanthi
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929)

p:forum_school_tabernae.summary: Elementary schools (ludi litterarum) were held in the shops round the Forum. Livy places the girl Verginia walking to school here in 449 BC when the decemvir Appius Claudius had her seized.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)

p:school_verrius_flaccus.summary: Augustus appointed the grammarian Verrius Flaccus to teach his grandsons, and moved his whole school into the atrium of the house of Catulus on the Palatine, on condition that he took no new pupils.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)

p:paedagogium_palatinum.summary: Building on the south-west slope of the Palatine above the Circus Maximus where the imperial slave pages were trained. Its walls carry hundreds of graffiti, among them the Alexamenos graffito mocking a Christian who worships a crucified donkey-headed figure.
scholarship: Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Paedagogium

p:auditorium_maecenatis.summary: Semi-sunken apsidal hall with tiered steps and garden frescoes in the Horti Maecenatis, found in 1874. Long called an auditorium for readings, it was probably a summer dining room with a water display; Horace and Virgil read in Maecenas' house.
scholarship: Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Auditorium Maecenatis

p:school_forum_traiani.summary: In late antiquity the Forum of Trajan with the Athenaeum nearby became the main teaching and recital place of the city: grammarians and rhetors taught here and poets recited before the Senate.
scholarship: Krautheimer, Rome: Profile of a City, 312-1308 (1980)
Marrou, A History of Education in Antiquity (1956)

p:school_justin_martyr.summary: Justin told the urban prefect Rusticus that he lived and taught 'above the baths of Myrtinus' during his stays in Rome; he was beheaded about 165.
scholarship: Lampe, From Paul to Valentinus (2003)
p:school_justin_martyr.note: Bath unidentified; placed on the Viminal by convention.

p:moneta_capitolina.summary: The Republican mint, in or beside the Temple of Juno Moneta on the Arx, from which our word money comes. Silver denarii were struck here from 211 BC under the tresviri monetales until production moved to the Caelian-Oppian valley under the Flavians.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Moneta
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929)
Crawford, Roman Republican Coinage (1974)

p:moneta_caesaris.summary: The imperial mint in Region III by the Via Labicana near San Clemente, where dedications of the mint officials of AD 115 were found. In 271 the moneyers led by Felicissimus revolted against Aurelian's reform and fought on the Caelian, with 7,000 soldiers killed. Coins were struck at Rome under the Ostrogoths and Byzantines.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Moneta
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)
Coarelli, Rome and Environs: An Archaeological Guide (2007)
p:moneta_caesaris.note: The large tufa building under San Clemente has been identified with it but this is uncertain.

p:subura_lupanaria.summary: The crowded valley between the Viminal and Esquiline had a reputation for brothels and night life; Martial and Juvenal use the 'wet' and noisy Subura as the image of vice, and the emperor's slaves and senators slummed here.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Subura
McGinn, The Economy of Prostitution in the Roman World (2004)
p:subura_lupanaria.note: The Regionary Catalogues count 45 or 46 lupanaria in the city.

p:summemmium.summary: District of cheap prostitution named several times by Martial; its location is unknown, though it is usually looked for near the Subura or the Esquiline.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Summemmium
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929)
McGinn, The Economy of Prostitution in the Roman World (2004)

p:circus_fornices.summary: Prostitutes, fortune-tellers and food sellers worked in the arcades under the seating of the Circus Maximus; the word fornix (arch) gave 'fornication'. Juvenal sends the foreign girls 'ordered to stand by the Circus'.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
McGinn, The Economy of Prostitution in the Roman World (2004)

p:venus_erycina_collina_festival.summary: Temple outside the Porta Collina (vowed 184, dedicated 181 BC) where on 23 April the prostitutes of the city offered myrtle, roses and incense to Venus.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Venus Erucina, Aedes

p:taberna_meritoria.summary: A hostel for veteran soldiers in Trastevere where in 38 BC oil was said to have gushed from the ground for a whole day (Fons Olei). The Historia Augusta has Severus Alexander award the site to the Christians rather than the tavern-keepers; Santa Maria in Trastevere stands here.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Taberna Meritoria
Krautheimer, Rome: Profile of a City, 312-1308 (1980)

p:tabernae_circi_maximi.summary: Shops and stalls under the arcades of the Circus Maximus at the end facing the Palatine and Caelian, full of flammable goods, where the Great Fire broke out on the night of 18-19 July 64.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)

p:velabrum_shops.summary: The Velabrum between the Forum and the river was a quarter of bakers, butchers, oil-sellers and wine shops. Plautus sends his characters there for food and Martial praises the cheese smoked in the Velabrum.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Velabrum
Holleran, Shopping in Ancient Rome (2012)

p:bookshops_argiletum.summary: The street from the Forum to the Subura beside the Curia was lined with cobblers and booksellers whose doorposts listed the titles on sale. Martial's publishers had shops here.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Argiletum
Holleran, Shopping in Ancient Rome (2012)

p:bookshop_atrectus.summary: Martial tells a friend not to send a slave to his house for his poems but to go to Atrectus' shop opposite the Forum of Caesar, its doorposts covered with advertisements, where a polished copy costs five denarii.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Holleran, Shopping in Ancient Rome (2012)

p:bookshop_secundus.summary: Martial advertises a pocket parchment edition of his poems at the shop of Secundus, freedman of the learned Lucensis, 'behind the threshold of Peace and the Forum of Pallas'.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Holleran, Shopping in Ancient Rome (2012)
p:bookshop_secundus.note: Between the Templum Pacis and the Forum Transitorium.

p:bookshops_vicus_sandaliarius.summary: Gellius describes a group of learned men gathered in the booksellers' quarter of the Vicus Sandaliarius when a self-styled expert on Sallust was exposed. The street also housed the sandal-makers.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Vicus Sandaliarius
Holleran, Shopping in Ancient Rome (2012)

p:bookshop_sosii.summary: Horace's publishers the Sosii brothers sold his books beside the statue of Vertumnus and the Ianus at the mouth of the Vicus Tuscus; Horace imagines his book eager to be 'on display, smoothed with the Sosii's pumice'.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Holleran, Shopping in Ancient Rome (2012)

p:sigillaria.summary: Market where clay figurines and small gifts were sold for the Saturnalia, and where Gellius found an old manuscript for sale in a bookshop. Often placed in the porticoes near the Baths of Trajan.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Sigillaria
Holleran, Shopping in Ancient Rome (2012)

p:saepta_market.summary: Once voting stopped, the enormous colonnaded voting enclosure became Rome's luxury bazaar. Martial's Mamurra spends a day here inspecting slave boys, tortoiseshell couches, Corinthian bronzes, crystal cups and murrhine ware, and buys two cheap cups.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Saepta Iulia
Holleran, Shopping in Ancient Rome (2012)
Haselberger et al., Mapping Augustan Rome (2002)

p:slave_market_castor.summary: Slave dealers (venalicii) displayed their merchandise near the Temple of Castor, the newcomers with chalked feet and a label round the neck; other dealers worked in the Saepta.
scholarship: Holleran, Shopping in Ancient Rome (2012)
Bodel, 'Slave labour and Roman society' (2011)

p:vicus_tuscus_market.summary: The street from the Forum to the Circus Maximus was Rome's luxury shopping street: perfumers and incense sellers (vicus turarius), silk dealers whose 'Tuscan' silks Martial mentions, and fashionable shoppers, but also shady characters Plautus places 'in Tusco vico'.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Vicus Tuscus
Holleran, Shopping in Ancient Rome (2012)

p:porticus_margaritaria.summary: Arcade of pearl and jewel dealers (margaritarii) on the Sacra Via, listed in Region VIII; inscriptions of margaritarii 'de Sacra Via' confirm the trade there.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Porticus Margaritaria
Holleran, Shopping in Ancient Rome (2012)
p:porticus_margaritaria.note: Placed on the Sacra Via below the Velia.

p:tabernae_novae.summary: Row of shops on the north side of the Forum, first butchers' stalls and then bankers' offices (argentariae), rebuilt after the fire of 210 BC and incorporated into the Basilica Aemilia's façade.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Tabernae Novae

p:tabernae_veteres.summary: The old row of shops on the south side of the Forum, cleared in 169 BC when Ti. Sempronius Gracchus bought Scipio Africanus' house and the shops behind for the Basilica Sempronia.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Tabernae Veteres

p:auction_halls.summary: Halls near the Forum where public and private auctions were held under the auctioneers (praecones); Cicero speaks of the Atria Licinia and the atria auctionaria, and an Atrium Auctionarium is listed among the sights of late-antique Rome.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Atria Licinia
Rauh, 'Auctioneers and the Roman economy', Historia 38 (1989)
p:auction_halls.note: Locations unknown; placed off the Argiletum.

p:atrium_sutorium.summary: Hall of the shoemakers where the trumpets of the priests were purified at the Tubilustrium on 23 March and 23 May.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Atrium Sutorium
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929)
p:atrium_sutorium.note: Site unknown; placed near the sandal-makers' Vicus Sandaliarius.

p:subura_market.summary: The Subura was also Rome's great everyday market: Martial lists the farm produce, eggs, fowl and vegetables his friend can buy there, and Juvenal's Umbricius complains of its din, carts and crowds.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Subura
Holleran, Shopping in Ancient Rome (2012)

p:clivus_argentarius_bankers.summary: The street from the Forum round the Capitol to the Campus Martius, named after the silversmiths and bankers who kept shops along it; the Basilica Argentaria of the Forum of Caesar opened onto it.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Clivus Argentarius
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929)

p:statio_marmorum_emporium.summary: The state marble depot on the river bank below the Aventine where imported blocks and columns from the imperial quarries were landed, registered with quarry marks and dressed; the riverside is still called Marmorata. Hundreds of abandoned blocks were found here in the 19th century.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Statio Marmorum
Fant, Cavum antrum Phrygiae (1989)
Maischberger, Marmor in Rom (1997)

p:marble_yard_campus_martius.summary: Second marble landing and workshop zone on the Tiber in the north-west Campus Martius near Tor di Nona and Sant'Apollinare, where large deposits of unworked marble and sculptors' workshops were found when the embankments were built.
scholarship: Maischberger, Marmor in Rom (1997)
Coarelli, Rome and Environs: An Archaeological Guide (2007)

p:figlinae_vaticanae.summary: The clay of the ager Vaticanus supplied potters and brickmakers; poets mock 'fragile Vatican plates' and the cheap wine of the Vatican slopes.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Vaticanus Ager
p:figlinae_vaticanae.note: Representative point; kilns were scattered along the valley below Monte Mario.

p:fullonica_casal_bertone.summary: The largest fullery-tannery complex known in the Roman world, excavated in 2006-2007 east of the city between the Via Praenestina and Tiburtina: over 1,000 square metres with about 100 vats for washing, dyeing and tanning, fed by an aqueduct branch.
scholarship: Musco and others, Le fullonicae di Casal Bertone (excavation reports, 2008)
Flohr, The World of the Fullo (2013)

p:coraria_septimiana.summary: Tanneries listed in Region XIV, presumably by the Porta Septimiana where the smell and the river water suited the trade, outside the main city across the Tiber.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Coraria Septimiana
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929)

p:tannery_s_cecilia.summary: Under Santa Cecilia in Trastevere excavations found a Republican house later converted to a tannery, with seven circular vats set in the floor, part of the industrial character of Trastevere.
scholarship: Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)

p:officinae_minii.summary: Workshops where cinnabar from the Spanish mines at Sisapo was refined into vermilion pigment, located between the temples of Flora and Quirinus on the Quirinal.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Officinae Minii

p:workshops_crypta_balbi.summary: In the ruined exedra of the Crypta Balbi, workshops of the late 6th-7th century produced belt fittings, glass, bone combs and metalwork for Roman and Lombard clients, one of the best-known industrial sites of early medieval Rome.
scholarship: Bertoldi and others in Manacorda (ed.), Museo Nazionale Romano Crypta Balbi (2000)
Ricci, 'Relazioni culturali e scambi commerciali nell'Italia centrale romano-longobarda' (1997)

p:spolia_lime_kilns.summary: As the population fell, marble from abandoned buildings was burned for lime and columns stripped for reuse. Majorian's law of 458 forbade the demolition of public buildings for materials; kilns later concentrated around Largo Argentina and the Crypta Balbi (the medieval Calcarario).
scholarship: Krautheimer, Rome: Profile of a City, 312-1308 (1980)
Bertoldi and others in Manacorda (ed.), Museo Nazionale Romano Crypta Balbi (2000)
p:spolia_lime_kilns.note: Most kilns found are 8th century or later; earlier dismantling is documented by laws.

p:portus_tiberinus.summary: The old river harbour of Rome on the left bank between the Pons Aemilius and the Forum Boarium, where barges unloaded before the Emporium below the Aventine was built in 193 BC. The Temple of Portunus guarded it.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Portus Tiberinus
Coarelli, Rome and Environs: An Archaeological Guide (2007)

p:navalia.summary: The state dockyards and shipsheds for the war fleet, where the ships of Perseus were displayed in 167 BC. Older scholarship placed them in the Campus Martius by Via Giulia; many now identify the great building at Testaccio long called the Porticus Aemilia as the Navalia.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Navalia
Cozza and Tucci, 'Navalia', ArchCl 57 (2006)
p:navalia.note: Placed at the Campus Martius hypothesis; see porticus_aemilia for the alternative.

p:ludus_matutinus.summary: Training school for the beast-hunters (venatores) who fought in the morning shows of the Colosseum, listed in Region II near the amphitheatre.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Ludus Matutinus
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000)
p:ludus_matutinus.note: Position south-east of the Ludus Magnus.

p:ludus_dacicus.summary: Gladiatorial school probably founded by Trajan for prisoners from his Dacian wars, listed in Region III near the Colosseum.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Ludus Dacicus
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000)

p:ludus_gallicus.summary: Gladiatorial school for fighters of the Gallic type, listed among the schools around the Colosseum.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Ludus Gallicus

p:summum_choragium.summary: Central store and workshop for stage scenery and machinery of the imperial games, in Region III near the Baths of Titus, with its own procurator.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Summum Choragium
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000)

p:armamentarium.summary: Armoury of the gladiatorial schools near the Colosseum.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Armamentarium

p:spoliarium_saniarium.summary: Rooms near the amphitheatre where dead gladiators were stripped (spoliarium) and the wounded treated (saniarium), listed in Region II.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Spoliarium

p:stabula_factionum.summary: Headquarters and stables of the four racing factions, the Whites, Reds, Greens and Blues, in the south-west Campus Martius near the later Palazzo Farnese and Via Giulia, with their own clubhouses, staff and horses.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Stabula IIII Factionum
Coarelli, Rome and Environs: An Archaeological Guide (2007)
p:stabula_factionum.note: Caligula dined and spent nights in the Greens' stable.

p:trigarium.summary: Open ground in the western Campus Martius where racehorses were exercised, near the factions' stables and the Tiber.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Trigarium
Coarelli, Rome and Environs: An Archaeological Guide (2007)

p:balneum_surae.summary: Baths built on the Aventine by L. Licinius Sura, Trajan's marshal, next to his house; a fragment of the Marble Plan shows them.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Thermae Suranae

p:thermae_novatianae.summary: Private bath of the 2nd century on the Vicus Patricius whose hall was converted into the church of Santa Pudenziana around 390; tradition linked it to the senator Pudens who hosted St Peter.
scholarship: Krautheimer, Rome: Profile of a City, 312-1308 (1980)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)

p:balnea_neratii_cerealis.summary: Baths built on the Esquiline in the mid-4th century by the consul Neratius Cerealis, near Santa Maria Maggiore, known from inscriptions.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Guidobaldi, 'Le domus tardoantiche di Roma', in Lavan and Bowden (eds), Theory and Practice in Late Antique Archaeology (2003)

p:lavacrum_agrippinae.summary: Bath on the Viminal named after Agrippina, listed in late sources and inscriptions concerning the water supply.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Lavacrum Agrippinae

p:thermae_severianae.summary: Baths that the Historia Augusta says Septimius Severus built in Trastevere near the gate named after him, the later Porta Settimiana.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Thermae Severianae

p:mithraeum_santa_prisca.summary: Mithraeum in the basement of a house on the Aventine, excavated by Vermaseren and van Essen in 1952-1966 under Santa Prisca. Painted processions of the seven grades of initiates and verses on its walls, one dated by the consuls of 202, make it the best documented Mithraic text in Rome. Christians smashed it around 400.
scholarship: Vermaseren, Corpus Inscriptionum et Monumentorum Religionis Mithriacae (1956-1960)
Clauss, The Roman Cult of Mithras (2000)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)
Vermaseren and van Essen, The Excavations in the Mithraeum of the Church of Santa Prisca (1965)

p:mithraeum_san_clemente.summary: Mithraeum in the courtyard of a 1st-century house next to the tufa building under San Clemente, with benches, a ceiling imitating a cave and an altar showing Mithras killing the bull. It was filled in when the first church was built over the neighbouring building in the late 4th century.
scholarship: Vermaseren, Corpus Inscriptionum et Monumentorum Religionis Mithriacae (1956-1960)
Clauss, The Roman Cult of Mithras (2000)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)
Guidobaldi, San Clemente: gli edifici romani (1992)

p:mithraeum_circus_maximus.summary: Mithraeum found in 1931 in the ground floor of a large public building near the starting gates of the Circus Maximus (under the former Pantanella pasta factory), with a marble relief of the bull-slaying still in place.
scholarship: Vermaseren, Corpus Inscriptionum et Monumentorum Religionis Mithriacae (1956-1960)
Clauss, The Roman Cult of Mithras (2000)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)

p:mithraeum_baths_caracalla.summary: The largest known mithraeum of Rome, in the vaulted service tunnels under the north-west corner of the Baths of Caracalla, found in 1912, with a pit perhaps used for initiation rites.
scholarship: Vermaseren, Corpus Inscriptionum et Monumentorum Religionis Mithriacae (1956-1960)
Clauss, The Roman Cult of Mithras (2000)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)
DeLaine, The Baths of Caracalla (1997)

p:mithraeum_castra_peregrina.summary: Mithraeum of the soldiers of the Castra Peregrina, found in 1973 under Santo Stefano Rotondo with painted and stucco decoration and marble reliefs.
scholarship: Vermaseren, Corpus Inscriptionum et Monumentorum Religionis Mithriacae (1956-1960)
Clauss, The Roman Cult of Mithras (2000)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)

p:mithraeum_barberini.summary: Mithraeum found in 1936 in the gardens of Palazzo Barberini on the Quirinal slope, with a large painted bull-slaying scene framed by the signs of the zodiac.
scholarship: Vermaseren, Corpus Inscriptionum et Monumentorum Religionis Mithriacae (1956-1960)
Clauss, The Roman Cult of Mithras (2000)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)

p:mithraeum_crypta_balbi.summary: Mithraeum installed in a building next to the Crypta Balbi in the 2nd century, found during the excavations of the 1980s-1990s.
scholarship: Vermaseren, Corpus Inscriptionum et Monumentorum Religionis Mithriacae (1956-1960)
Clauss, The Roman Cult of Mithras (2000)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)
Bertoldi and others in Manacorda (ed.), Museo Nazionale Romano Crypta Balbi (2000)

p:mithraeum_via_lanza.summary: Mithraeum discovered in 1885 on the Esquiline during the building of the new quarter, with sculpture and inscriptions now in the Capitoline collections.
scholarship: Vermaseren, Corpus Inscriptionum et Monumentorum Religionis Mithriacae (1956-1960)
Clauss, The Roman Cult of Mithras (2000)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)
p:mithraeum_via_lanza.note: Exact position on the street approximate.

p:phrygianum_vatican.summary: Sanctuary of Cybele and Attis on the Vatican plain where taurobolia were performed; altars dated 295-390 recording the bull-sacrifices of leading pagan senators were found in 1609 under the façade of St Peter's.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Phrygianum
Salzman, The Making of a Christian Aristocracy (2002)

p:dolichenum_aventine.summary: Sanctuary of Jupiter Dolichenus, the Syrian god of soldiers, found in 1935 near Sant'Alessio, with many dedications and statues.
scholarship: Chini, Il santuario di Iuppiter Dolichenus sull'Aventino (1997)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)

p:syrian_sanctuary_janiculum.summary: Sanctuary on the Janiculum at Villa Sciarra, first the grove of the nymph Furrina where Gaius Gracchus died in 121 BC, then in the 2nd-4th centuries a temple of Syrian gods (Hadad and Atargatis) with a bronze-gilt statue of a mummy-like figure wrapped by a snake.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Lucus Furrinae
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)
Goddard, 'The tomb of the Syrian gods', excavation reports (2008)

p:iseum_metellinum.summary: Temple of Isis in Region III, from which the region took its name 'Isis et Serapis', probably on the slope of the Oppian along the Via Labicana; the name suggests a founder of the Metellus family.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Isis, Aedes (Metellina)
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929)

p:jewish_quarter_trastevere.summary: Philo, who came to Rome in 40, says the Jews of Rome lived mostly across the Tiber, most of them freedmen brought as captives by Pompey, with their own prayer houses. The Monteverde catacomb above the Via Portuensis served them.
scholarship: Rutgers, The Jews in Late Ancient Rome (1995)
Noy, Jewish Inscriptions of Western Europe II: The City of Rome (1995)

p:jewish_porta_capena.summary: Juvenal complains that the sacred grove of Egeria by the Porta Capena had been let to Jews 'whose furniture is a basket and some hay'.
scholarship: Rutgers, The Jews in Late Ancient Rome (1995)

p:synagogue_siburesians.summary: One of at least eleven synagogue congregations named in the Jewish catacomb epitaphs of Rome; the Siburesians took their name from the Subura.
scholarship: Noy, Jewish Inscriptions of Western Europe II: The City of Rome (1995)
Rutgers, The Jews in Late Ancient Rome (1995)
p:synagogue_siburesians.note: No synagogue building has been found in Rome; placed in the Subura from the name.

p:synagogue_campesians.summary: Congregation named in catacomb epitaphs after the Campus Martius district.
scholarship: Noy, Jewish Inscriptions of Western Europe II: The City of Rome (1995)
Rutgers, The Jews in Late Ancient Rome (1995)
p:synagogue_campesians.note: Placed in the Campus Martius from the name.

p:synagogue_augustesians.summary: Congregation named after Augustus, perhaps of imperial freedmen, attested in epitaphs; with the Agrippesians and Volumnesians among the oldest synagogues of Rome.
scholarship: Noy, Jewish Inscriptions of Western Europe II: The City of Rome (1995)
Rutgers, The Jews in Late Ancient Rome (1995)
p:synagogue_augustesians.note: Unlocated; placed in the Trastevere quarter.

p:synagogue_agrippesians.summary: Congregation named after Agrippa (Marcus Agrippa or Herod Agrippa), attested in epitaphs.
scholarship: Noy, Jewish Inscriptions of Western Europe II: The City of Rome (1995)
Rutgers, The Jews in Late Ancient Rome (1995)
p:synagogue_agrippesians.note: Unlocated; placed in the Trastevere quarter.

p:titulus_aemilianae.summary: Named in the synod of 595; the church of the Four Crowned Martyrs on the Caelian, rebuilt in the 9th century. One of the 25 titular churches, the parish churches of Rome whose priests signed the synod of 499.

sources.a: Acts of the Roman synod of 499

scholarship: Hülsen, Le chiese di Roma nel medio evo (1927)
Pietri, Roma Christiana (1976)
Krautheimer, Rome: Profile of a City, 312-1308 (1980)
p:titulus_aemilianae.note: From-date is the first secure attestation or building date; many tituli began as halls in private houses whose dates are unknown.

p:titulus_anastasiae.summary: Church at the foot of the Palatine by the Circus Maximus, built in the 4th century over a house and shops; later the church of the Byzantine court on the Palatine. One of the 25 titular churches, the parish churches of Rome whose priests signed the synod of 499.

sources.a: Acts of the Roman synod of 499

scholarship: Hülsen, Le chiese di Roma nel medio evo (1927)
Pietri, Roma Christiana (1976)
Krautheimer, Rome: Profile of a City, 312-1308 (1980)
p:titulus_anastasiae.note: From-date is the first secure attestation or building date; many tituli began as halls in private houses whose dates are unknown.

p:titulus_eudoxiae.summary: Church of the Apostles on the Oppian, rebuilt around 439 by Sixtus III with the empress Eudoxia's support to house the chains of Peter. One of the 25 titular churches, the parish churches of Rome whose priests signed the synod of 499.

sources.a: Acts of the Roman synod of 499

scholarship: Hülsen, Le chiese di Roma nel medio evo (1927)
Pietri, Roma Christiana (1976)
Krautheimer, Rome: Profile of a City, 312-1308 (1980)
p:titulus_eudoxiae.note: From-date is the first secure attestation or building date; many tituli began as halls in private houses whose dates are unknown.

p:titulus_byzantis_pammachii.summary: Basilica built about 410 by the senator Pammachius over the houses on the Clivus Scauri where tradition placed the martyrdom of John and Paul. One of the 25 titular churches, the parish churches of Rome whose priests signed the synod of 499.

sources.a: Acts of the Roman synod of 499

scholarship: Hülsen, Le chiese di Roma nel medio evo (1927)
Pietri, Roma Christiana (1976)
Krautheimer, Rome: Profile of a City, 312-1308 (1980)
p:titulus_byzantis_pammachii.note: From-date is the first secure attestation or building date; many tituli began as halls in private houses whose dates are unknown.

p:titulus_caeciliae.summary: Church in Trastevere over a Roman house said to be that of the martyr Cecilia. One of the 25 titular churches, the parish churches of Rome whose priests signed the synod of 499.

sources.a: Acts of the Roman synod of 499

scholarship: Hülsen, Le chiese di Roma nel medio evo (1927)
Pietri, Roma Christiana (1976)
Krautheimer, Rome: Profile of a City, 312-1308 (1980)
p:titulus_caeciliae.note: From-date is the first secure attestation or building date; many tituli began as halls in private houses whose dates are unknown.

p:titulus_iulii_callisti.summary: Basilica of Pope Julius I (337-352) on the site of the Taberna Meritoria, linked by tradition to Pope Callixtus. One of the 25 titular churches, the parish churches of Rome whose priests signed the synod of 499.

sources.a: Acts of the Roman synod of 499

scholarship: Hülsen, Le chiese di Roma nel medio evo (1927)
Pietri, Roma Christiana (1976)
Krautheimer, Rome: Profile of a City, 312-1308 (1980)
p:titulus_iulii_callisti.note: From-date is the first secure attestation or building date; many tituli began as halls in private houses whose dates are unknown.

p:titulus_clementis.summary: Basilica built in the late 4th century over a 1st-century building and the adjoining mithraeum, named after Clement, third successor of Peter. One of the 25 titular churches, the parish churches of Rome whose priests signed the synod of 499.

sources.a: Acts of the Roman synod of 499

scholarship: Hülsen, Le chiese di Roma nel medio evo (1927)
Pietri, Roma Christiana (1976)
Krautheimer, Rome: Profile of a City, 312-1308 (1980)
p:titulus_clementis.note: From-date is the first secure attestation or building date; many tituli began as halls in private houses whose dates are unknown.

p:titulus_crescentianae.summary: Titulus on the Via Appia near the Baths of Caracalla, later dedicated to Pope Sixtus II. One of the 25 titular churches, the parish churches of Rome whose priests signed the synod of 499.

sources.a: Acts of the Roman synod of 499

scholarship: Hülsen, Le chiese di Roma nel medio evo (1927)
Pietri, Roma Christiana (1976)
Krautheimer, Rome: Profile of a City, 312-1308 (1980)
