p:diaconia_s_maria_antiqua.summary: Church in the Augustan hall at the foot of the Palatine, converted in the mid-6th century, perhaps serving the Byzantine officials on the Palatine. It had become a diaconia, a welfare station distributing food, by the 7th century.
scholarship: Krautheimer, Rome: Profile of a City, 312-1308 (1980)
Osborne, Brandt and Morganti (eds), Santa Maria Antiqua al Foro Romano (2004)

p:diaconia_s_maria_cosmedin.summary: The Statio Annonae by the Forum Boarium was turned into a diaconia in the late 6th century, continuing in church hands the food distribution once run by the state.
scholarship: Krautheimer, Rome: Profile of a City, 312-1308 (1980)
Durliat, De la ville antique à la ville byzantine (1990)

p:diaconia_s_teodoro.summary: Round church at the foot of the Palatine on the old Horrea Agrippiana, with a 6th-7th century apse mosaic; later a diaconia.
scholarship: Krautheimer, Rome: Profile of a City, 312-1308 (1980)
Hülsen, Le chiese di Roma nel medio evo (1927)

p:diaconia_s_maria_via_lata.summary: Welfare station installed in the ground floor of the late Roman warehouse on the Via Lata, with 7th-century paintings.
scholarship: Krautheimer, Rome: Profile of a City, 312-1308 (1980)

p:diaconia_s_maria_domnica.summary: Diaconia on the Caelian over the station of the fifth cohort of vigiles, rebuilt by Paschal I in the 9th century.
scholarship: Krautheimer, Rome: Profile of a City, 312-1308 (1980)
Hülsen, Le chiese di Roma nel medio evo (1927)

p:xenodochium_belisarii.summary: Hostel for travellers and the poor founded by Belisarius on the Via Lata during the Gothic siege, with the church of Santa Maria in Trivio, according to the Liber Pontificalis as penance for deposing Pope Silverius.
scholarship: Krautheimer, Rome: Profile of a City, 312-1308 (1980)

p:xenodochium_valerii.summary: Hospice on the Caelian on the site of the great Domus Valeriorum, which Melania the Younger had been unable to sell before 410; it is attested later as the 'xenodochium Valerii'.
scholarship: Krautheimer, Rome: Profile of a City, 312-1308 (1980)
Guidobaldi, 'Le domus tardoantiche di Roma', in Lavan and Bowden (eds), Theory and Practice in Late Antique Archaeology (2003)

p:hospice_symmachus_st_peter.summary: Pope Symmachus (498-514) built lodgings for the poor beside the basilicas of St Peter, St Paul and St Lawrence, the first papal charitable buildings at the great shrines.
scholarship: Krautheimer, Rome: Profile of a City, 312-1308 (1980)

p:hospice_symmachus_st_paul.summary: Lodgings for the poor built by Symmachus beside San Paolo fuori le mura.
scholarship: Krautheimer, Rome: Profile of a City, 312-1308 (1980)

p:hospice_symmachus_st_lawrence.summary: Lodgings for the poor built by Symmachus beside San Lorenzo fuori le mura on the Via Tiburtina.
scholarship: Krautheimer, Rome: Profile of a City, 312-1308 (1980)

p:nosocomium_fabiolae.summary: The noble widow Fabiola founded the first Christian hospital in Rome in the 390s, gathering the sick from the streets and nursing them herself, as Jerome records in his obituary letter.
scholarship: Krautheimer, Rome: Profile of a City, 312-1308 (1980)
p:nosocomium_fabiolae.note: Location unknown; placed near the Lateran by convention.

p:tiber_island_sickhouse.summary: The sick slept in the porticoes of the Temple of Aesculapius hoping for a healing dream; masters abandoned sick slaves here, and Claudius ruled that slaves so abandoned who recovered were free.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Aesculapius, Aedes
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)

p:monastery_st_andrew.summary: Gregory the Great turned his family house on the Clivus Scauri into a monastery dedicated to St Andrew in about 575 and lived there as a monk; from here Augustine and his companions left in 596 for the mission to England.
scholarship: Krautheimer, Rome: Profile of a City, 312-1308 (1980)
Markus, Gregory the Great and his World (1997)
p:monastery_st_andrew.note: Now San Gregorio Magno al Celio.

p:esquiline_necropolis.summary: The great cemetery outside the Esquiline gate, used from the Iron Age. By the late Republic it included the puticuli, open pits into which the bodies of slaves and the destitute were thrown with rubbish; Lanciani found pits full of bones and refuse in the 1870s. Maecenas covered it with earth and laid out his gardens around 35 BC.
scholarship: Lanciani, Forma Urbis Romae (1893-1901)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Esquiliae
Graham, Death, Disposal and the Destitute (2006)

p:esquiline_fresco_tomb.summary: Chamber tomb on the Esquiline found in 1875 with the earliest Roman historical painting (c. 300-250 BC): Q. Fabius and M. Fannius parleying in scenes of the Samnite wars, perhaps from the tomb of the Fabii.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Coarelli, 'Il sepolcro degli Scipioni' and studies on the Esquiline fresco (1976)

p:vatican_necropolis.summary: Street of mausolea of freedmen and Christians on the slope of the Vatican hill north of the Circus of Gaius and Nero, excavated under St Peter's in 1940-1949. Its focus is the 2nd-century aedicula (Trophy of Gaius) over a poor grave revered as Peter's. Constantine filled it in to build the basilica.
scholarship: Toynbee and Ward-Perkins, The Shrine of St Peter and the Vatican Excavations (1956)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)

p:via_triumphalis_necropolis.summary: Cemetery of slaves, freedmen and craftsmen along the Via Triumphalis on the Vatican slope, excavated under the Vatican car park and the Santa Rosa area (2003-2006), with hundreds of modest graves and small tombs.
scholarship: Liverani and Spinola, The Vatican Necropoles (2010)

p:via_ostiensis_necropolis.summary: Cemetery along the road to Ostia, of which a stretch with columbaria and tombs survives near San Paolo; Paul was buried in it and Constantine's basilica rose over his grave.
scholarship: Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)
Liverani and Spinola, The Vatican Necropoles (2010)

p:via_salaria_necropolis.summary: Tombs along the Salaria and Pinciana outside the Aurelian Wall, including the drum mausoleum of Lucilius Paetus and his daughter (c. 10 BC) and the tomb of the boy poet Q. Sulpicius Maximus by the Porta Salaria.
scholarship: Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)

p:via_flaminia_necropolis.summary: Tombs lining the Via Flaminia beyond the Porta Flaminia, among them the family tomb of the Domitii on the Pincian slope where Nero's ashes were laid.
scholarship: Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)

p:via_latina_necropolis.summary: Archaeological park of tombs along the Via Latina, including the painted and stuccoed tombs of the Valerii and the Pancratii (2nd century).
scholarship: Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)

p:via_portuensis_necropolis.summary: Cemeteries along the Via Portuensis and the slopes of Monteverde, with columbaria, the Jewish catacomb and the Christian catacomb of Pontianus.
scholarship: Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)

p:sepulcretum_statiliorum.summary: Burial chambers of the slaves and freedmen of the Statilii Tauri on the Esquiline near the Porta Maggiore, found in 1875 with hundreds of epitaphs and a painted frieze of Rome's foundation legends.
scholarship: Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)

p:columbaria_vigna_codini.summary: Three large underground columbaria of the early empire near the Porta San Sebastiano, one with niches for some 500 urns of imperial slaves and freedmen.
scholarship: Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)

p:columbarium_pomponius_hylas.summary: Small columbarium of the early 1st century near the Tomb of the Scipios, with a glass mosaic panel naming Pomponius Hylas and his wife Vitalis, and fine paintings.
scholarship: Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)

p:columbarium_liviae.summary: Columbarium of the household of Livia found in 1726 on the Via Appia inside the later Aurelian Wall, with over 1,000 urns and epitaphs listing slave jobs from hairdressers to accountants.
scholarship: Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)
Treggiari, 'Jobs in the household of Livia', PBSR 43 (1975)

p:hypogeum_aurelii.summary: Underground family tomb of the 3rd century on Viale Manzoni, found in 1919, with paintings mixing Christian, Gnostic and classical imagery.
scholarship: Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)
Fiocchi Nicolai, Bisconti and Mazzoleni, The Christian Catacombs of Rome (1999)

p:basilica_porta_maggiore.summary: Three-aisled underground hall of the 1st century with white stucco reliefs of myths of the soul, found in 1917 under the railway. Its use (Neopythagorean sect, funerary hall of the Statilii) is debated; it seems to have been filled in soon after building.
scholarship: Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)
Carcopino, La basilique pythagoricienne de la Porte Majeure (1926)

p:catacomb_priscilla.summary: One of the oldest Christian cemeteries, developed from a quarry and a hypogeum of the Acilii Glabriones; it holds the earliest image of the Virgin and Child (early 3rd century) and the 'Greek chapel'. Seven popes were buried here.
scholarship: Fiocchi Nicolai, Bisconti and Mazzoleni, The Christian Catacombs of Rome (1999)
Nestori, Repertorio topografico delle pitture delle catacombe romane (1993)
p:catacomb_priscilla.note: Coordinates approximate to the main entrance. Burials ceased in the early 5th century but martyr shrines were visited by pilgrims through the 7th century.

p:catacomb_domitilla.summary: Vast catacomb on land of Flavia Domitilla, with the semi-subterranean basilica of Nereus and Achilleus (late 4th century) and some 15 km of galleries.

p:catacomb_domitilla.note: Coordinates approximate to the main entrance. Burials ceased in the early 5th century but martyr shrines were visited by pilgrims through the 7th century.

p:catacomb_callixtus.note: Coordinates approximate to the main entrance. Burials ceased in the early 5th century but martyr shrines were visited by pilgrims through the 7th century.

Noy, Jewish Inscriptions of Western Europe II: The City of Rome (1995)
p:catacomb_monteverde_jewish.note: Coordinates approximate to the main entrance. Burials ceased in the early 5th century but martyr shrines were visited by pilgrims through the 7th century.

p:domus_valerii_publicolae.summary: When the people suspected that the consul Valerius was building a fortress-like house on the summit of the Velia above the Forum, he had it pulled down overnight and rebuilt at the foot of the hill, earning the name Publicola.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Carandini (ed.), The Atlas of Ancient Rome (2017)

p:domus_spurii_cassii.summary: The house of the consul Spurius Cassius, executed in 485 BC for aiming at kingship, was razed; the Temple of Tellus later rose on the empty site on the Carinae.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Carandini (ed.), The Atlas of Ancient Rome (2017)

p:domus_spurii_maelii.summary: Maelius, a rich knight who sold grain cheaply during a famine, was killed in 439 BC as a would-be tyrant; his house was demolished and the empty plot below the Capitol was called the Aequimaelium.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Carandini (ed.), The Atlas of Ancient Rome (2017)

p:domus_manlii_capitolini.summary: The saviour of the Capitol from the Gauls lived on the Arx; after his execution in 384 BC his house was razed and patricians were forbidden to live on the Capitol. The Temple of Juno Moneta was later built on the site.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Carandini (ed.), The Atlas of Ancient Rome (2017)

p:domus_vitruvii_vacci.summary: The house on the Palatine of Vitruvius Vaccus of Fundi, executed after his revolt in 330 BC, was razed and the site left open as the 'meadows of Vaccus'.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Carandini (ed.), The Atlas of Ancient Rome (2017)

p:domus_scipionis_africani.summary: Scipio Africanus lived behind the Tabernae Veteres near the statue of Vortumnus; in 169 BC Ti. Sempronius Gracchus bought the house and the shops behind it to build the Basilica Sempronia.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Carandini (ed.), The Atlas of Ancient Rome (2017)

p:domus_fulvii_flacci.summary: The house on the Palatine of Fulvius Flaccus, killed with Gaius Gracchus in 121 BC, was razed; Q. Lutatius Catulus built a portico on the site with spoils from the Cimbric war, which Clodius later tried to merge into his shrine of Libertas.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Carandini (ed.), The Atlas of Ancient Rome (2017)

p:domus_gai_gracchi.summary: Gaius Gracchus moved from his house on the Palatine to the district below the Forum where the poor and humble lived, to show himself a man of the people.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Carandini (ed.), The Atlas of Ancient Rome (2017)
p:domus_gai_gracchi.note: Precise district unknown; placed between the Forum and the Subura.

p:domus_crassi_oratoris.summary: The orator Crassus (cos. 95 BC) shocked contemporaries with six columns of Hymettian marble in his Palatine house and famous lotus trees in its garden; the censor Ahenobarbus mocked him as the 'Palatine Venus'.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Carandini (ed.), The Atlas of Ancient Rome (2017)

p:domus_ciceronis.summary: Cicero bought the house of M. Livius Drusus on the north slope of the Palatine above the Forum from Crassus in 62 BC for 3.5 million sesterces. Clodius burned it during Cicero's exile in 58 and built a shrine of Libertas on part of the site; the Senate restored the land in 57 and Cicero rebuilt.

phases.t: burned by Clodius; shrine of Libertas
site restored and rebuilt

scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Carandini (ed.), The Atlas of Ancient Rome (2017)
p:domus_ciceronis.note: Located by its view over the Forum; remains under the Domus Tiberiana's north-east slope have been proposed.

p:domus_clodii.summary: Clodius bought the neighbouring house of Scaurus for 14.8 million sesterces, intending to join it to Cicero's former site, before his death on the Via Appia in 52 BC.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Carandini (ed.), The Atlas of Ancient Rome (2017)

p:domus_scauri.summary: The aedile of 58 BC moved the 38-foot marble columns of his temporary theatre into the atrium of his house on the Palatine slope below the Sacra Via. Carandini's excavations identified a large atrium house at the north-east foot of the Palatine as Scaurus'.
scholarship: Carandini (ed.), The Atlas of Ancient Rome (2017)
Carandini and Carafa, Palatium e Sacra Via I (1995)

p:domus_pompeii_carinae.summary: Pompey's ancestral, modest house on the Carinae, decorated with ships' beaks. After his death Mark Antony took it and Cicero mocked him for it; Tiberius later lived there before moving to the Gardens of Maecenas.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Carandini (ed.), The Atlas of Ancient Rome (2017)

p:domus_caesaris_subura.summary: Before his election as pontifex maximus in 63 BC, when he moved into the Domus Publica on the Sacra Via, Caesar lived in a modest house in the Subura.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Carandini (ed.), The Atlas of Ancient Rome (2017)

p:domus_attici.summary: Cicero's friend Atticus lived on the Quirinal in the Tamphilian house he inherited from his uncle, more charming for its grove than its buildings.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Carandini (ed.), The Atlas of Ancient Rome (2017)
p:domus_attici.note: Near the Temple of Quirinus and the Temple of Salus.

p:domus_augusti_natalis.summary: Augustus was born in September 63 BC in a house at the 'Ox-heads' at the north-east corner of the Palatine, later made a shrine.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Carandini (ed.), The Atlas of Ancient Rome (2017)

p:domus_agrippae.summary: Augustus gave the former house of Mark Antony on the Palatine jointly to Agrippa and Valerius Messalla after it burned.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Carandini (ed.), The Atlas of Ancient Rome (2017)

p:domus_maecenatis.summary: Maecenas built his mansion with a high tower on the Esquiline over the filled-in necropolis; Horace invites the reader to look down from it on the smoke and wealth of Rome, and Nero watched the Great Fire from the 'tower of Maecenas'.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Carandini (ed.), The Atlas of Ancient Rome (2017)

p:domus_vergilii.summary: Virgil had a house on the Esquiline next to the gardens of Maecenas.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Carandini (ed.), The Atlas of Ancient Rome (2017)

p:domus_ovidii.summary: In the poem on his last night in Rome Ovid looks out at the Capitol, the temple 'near our house'.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Carandini (ed.), The Atlas of Ancient Rome (2017)

p:domus_lateranorum.summary: Mansion on the Caelian of Plautius Lateranus, consul-designate executed in the Pisonian conspiracy of 65; confiscated, it passed to the emperors and gave its name to the Lateran. Remains lie under the Lateran hospital.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)

p:domus_flaviorum_malum_punicum.summary: Domitian was born in 51 in his father Vespasian's house on the Quirinal at the 'Pomegranate'; he later turned it into the Templum Gentis Flaviae, the family mausoleum.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Carandini (ed.), The Atlas of Ancient Rome (2017)

p:domus_martialis.summary: Martial lived on the Quirinal near the 'Pear Tree', up three high flights of stairs, before he acquired a small house and returned to Spain in 98.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Carandini (ed.), The Atlas of Ancient Rome (2017)

p:domus_plinii_minoris.summary: Pliny's town house stood on the Esquiline near the Lacus Orphei, at the top of the slope beyond the Subura; Martial sends his book there.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Carandini (ed.), The Atlas of Ancient Rome (2017)

p:domus_licinii_surae.summary: Trajan's marshal L. Licinius Sura had a house on the Aventine beside his baths overlooking the Circus Maximus.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Carandini (ed.), The Atlas of Ancient Rome (2017)

p:privata_traiani.summary: Trajan's house before his accession, listed in Region XIII on the Aventine. The house with fine paintings under Santa Prisca has been proposed.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Carandini (ed.), The Atlas of Ancient Rome (2017)

p:domus_marci_aurelii.summary: Marcus Aurelius was born in 121 in the gardens of his family on the Caelian near the house of Lateranus, where an equestrian statue, perhaps the Capitoline one, later stood.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Carandini (ed.), The Atlas of Ancient Rome (2017)

p:domus_vectiliana.summary: House on the Caelian to which Commodus moved, saying he could not sleep in the palace; he was strangled there on 31 December 192.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Carandini (ed.), The Atlas of Ancient Rome (2017)

p:domus_cilonis.summary: Mansion of L. Fabius Cilo, urban prefect and friend of Septimius Severus, listed in Region XII on the Piccolo Aventino; remains are associated with Santa Balbina.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Domus Cilonis
Guidobaldi, 'Le domus tardoantiche di Roma', in Lavan and Bowden (eds), Theory and Practice in Late Antique Archaeology (2003)

p:domus_tetricorum.summary: After his surrender to Aurelian the Gallic emperor Tetricus lived in Rome in a fine house on the Caelian 'between the two groves opposite the Temple of Isis Metellina', with a mosaic showing Aurelian investing him.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Carandini (ed.), The Atlas of Ancient Rome (2017)

p:domus_faustae.summary: The house of the empress Fausta at the Lateran, where Pope Miltiades held the synod of October 313 against the Donatists.
scholarship: Krautheimer, Rome: Profile of a City, 312-1308 (1980)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)

p:domus_symmachi.summary: Town house on the Caelian of Q. Aurelius Symmachus, urban prefect and orator, leader of the pagan senators in the Altar of Victory affair; inscriptions honouring the family were found on the hill.
scholarship: Guidobaldi, 'Le domus tardoantiche di Roma', in Lavan and Bowden (eds), Theory and Practice in Late Antique Archaeology (2003)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
p:domus_symmachi.note: His house in Trastevere was attacked by a mob in a grain shortage.

p:domus_valeriorum.summary: Palatial house of the Valerii on the Caelian near Santo Stefano Rotondo. Melania the Younger and Pinianus tried to sell it to give the money to the poor, but no one in Rome could afford it; after the sack of 410 it was sold cheaply. Parts with bronze patronage tablets were found in 1554 and 1902.
scholarship: Guidobaldi, 'Le domus tardoantiche di Roma', in Lavan and Bowden (eds), Theory and Practice in Late Antique Archaeology (2003)
Krautheimer, Rome: Profile of a City, 312-1308 (1980)
p:domus_valeriorum.note: Identical with the 'house of Valerius' and 'house of Melania' on the Caelian; later the xenodochium Valerii.

p:domus_gaudentii.summary: Late-antique house on the Caelian known from an inscription naming Gaudentius, one of the aristocratic mansions that covered the hill in the 4th century.
scholarship: Guidobaldi, 'Le domus tardoantiche di Roma', in Lavan and Bowden (eds), Theory and Practice in Late Antique Archaeology (2003)

p:domus_marcellae.summary: The widow Marcella turned her Aventine house into a centre of ascetic study where Jerome taught. When the Goths entered in 410 they beat her to make her reveal hidden gold; she died soon after at St Paul's.
scholarship: Krautheimer, Rome: Profile of a City, 312-1308 (1980)

p:case_romane_celio.summary: A 2nd-century apartment block with shops on the Clivus Scauri, joined in the 3rd-4th centuries into one rich house with painted rooms and a small Christian confessio. Pammachius built the basilica of Santi Giovanni e Paolo over it around 410.
scholarship: Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)
Guidobaldi, 'Le domus tardoantiche di Roma', in Lavan and Bowden (eds), Theory and Practice in Late Antique Archaeology (2003)

p:domus_pinciana.summary: Great late-antique house on the Pincian, by the Aurelian Wall, perhaps of the Anicii Probi; Belisarius made it his headquarters during the Gothic siege of 537-538, and Pope Silverius was summoned and deposed there.
scholarship: Krautheimer, Rome: Profile of a City, 312-1308 (1980)
Guidobaldi, 'Le domus tardoantiche di Roma', in Lavan and Bowden (eds), Theory and Practice in Late Antique Archaeology (2003)

p:domus_gregorii.summary: The house of Gregory's family, of senatorial rank, on the Clivus Scauri facing the Palatine, which he converted into the monastery of St Andrew around 575.
scholarship: Krautheimer, Rome: Profile of a City, 312-1308 (1980)

p:domus_palazzo_valentini.summary: Two aristocratic houses of the 2nd-4th centuries with baths, mosaics and polychrome marble floors excavated under Palazzo Valentini near Trajan's Column, now a museum.
scholarship: Baldassarri (ed.), Palazzo Valentini: l'area archeologica (2008)

p:domus_pudentis.summary: Tradition held that the senator Pudens hosted Peter in his house on the Vicus Patricius; the 2nd-century bath and house remains below Santa Pudenziana gave rise to the story.
scholarship: Krautheimer, Rome: Profile of a City, 312-1308 (1980)
